#6736. Only Law Roach Could Source a Look From Marc Jacobs’s Louis Vuitton x Richard Prince Collab

Law Roach’s latest archival pull for Kim Kardashian was for the fashion (and art) history buffs.

In October of 2007, Marc Jacobs sent models down the Louis Vuitton runway dressed as an army of over-the-top 1950s-inspired nurses. As seen on the likes of Naomi Campbell, Stephanie Seymour, Eva Herzigova, and Nadja Auermann, baggy plastic coats were layered over colorful dresses and cinched with leather belts, and black lace masks were embroidered with the house’s logo. Each uniform was styled with white tights and white heels, and topped with traditional nurse’s caps—stitched with red sequin letters that together spelled out “Louis Vuitton.”

The campy Spring/Summer 2008 collection, presented during Paris Fashion Week under the helm of then-artistic director Jacobs, was inspired by Richard Prince’s 2003 “Nurse Paintings” series. The pop artist, who rose to prominence in the 1980s, shared Jacobs’s love for a reference—and for this particular body of work, he transformed the covers of mid-20th century medical pulp novels into eery, gory paintings, with messy paint runs and blurry red splotches that read as blood.

The result was a vibrant commentary on society’s portrayal of women as both pure caregivers and sexualized fetishes—an idea which further came to life on the LV models.

(One such painting was even featured on the cover of a Sonic Youth album, 2004’s Sonic Nurse.)

Nearly two decades later, the seminal collection returned to the fashion discourse thanks to Roach (and Kardashian). The stylist, a dedicated archivist who has pulled rare vintage gems for everyone from Zendaya to Ariana Grande, dressed the All’s Fair actor as a Louis Vuitton nurse.

The Spring/Summer 2008 ensemble was complete with the season’s Papillon Frame bag, made in collaboration with Prince, and the duo even worked with milliner Stephen Jones on a custom “K” headpiece.

#6734. Burberry Retail Sales Grow 4% in Q2, Carried by China and the US

Burberry’s comparable retail sales grew 4% on a constant currency basis in both the second quarter and first half of the fiscal year 2026/2027. For H1, Burberry’s group revenues grew 6% to €1.1 billion.

“Two years ago, we launched Burberry Forward [a plan to bring the brand back to where it was four years ago with a focus on outerwear and a diversified pricing structure]. Today, our brand is stronger, and our business is healthier,” said CEO Joshua Schulman on Thursday’s call. “We have delivered five consecutive quarters of growth and improved our quality of sales, which demonstrates that our strategy is working. This momentum stretches across product categories, channels, and geographies, and has translated into higher gross margin and increased profitability.”

Adjusted operating profit reached £62 million in H1, while gross margin rose to 68.3% — up 40 basis points from 67.9%.

Regionally, the Americas took the lion’s share of retail growth in Q2, up 11%, driven by local spending and activations, and healthy in-store conversion. Greater China followed, up 5% in Q2, a deceleration from Q1’s 9% climb. Burberry attributed this industry outperformance, in part, to the strong appeal of Burberry as a British heritage brand.

“We know that there’s been a lot of news about the challenging luxury market in China, but we’re being very deliberate, continuing to invest in our relationships with our customers in that part of the world,” said Schulman. “We understand that luxury customers around the world — particularly in China — are experiencing fatigue with exorbitant pricing, and in this context, our strategy of having enduring value and providing great value for money is resonating strongly with the Chinese customers.”

The Asia-Pacific region, excluding China, also grew in the quarter, up 3%, with South Korea growing 12%, driven by local demand. Japan was a weak point, down 1% in the quarter, attributed to softer tourism from mainland China. EMEIA also dropped 2%, due to softer tourism and traffic.

“It’s no secret that global tourism is down. So the local customer has been spending in their respective regions. We’re seeing globally that Middle Eastern, Chinese, European, and British customers are shopping at home,” said Schulman. “This is a trend we’ve been seeing all year long. There’s just less cross-border travel than there has been in the past.”

By category, womenswear led growth across retail and wholesale, growing 9%, followed by accessories (6%). Childrenswear and other also grew (5%), as well as menswear (3%).

The company didn’t share figures for outerwear, but reported double-digit retail growth in H1, led by the “rainwear” category. Lightweight gabardine designs and shorter styles performed through summer, while new cashmere and leather launches showed traction towards the end of Q2. Accessories also grew in Q2, and leather goods accelerated, boosted by strong performance in women’s handbags — particularly the vintage check and Cotswolds ranges.

Wholesale revenue grew 17% in H1. The company attributed this performance to the confidence of its partners, who are achieving high sell-throughs of Burberry products and continuing to invest in the brand’s designs. Licensing revenues dropped 5%. The brand opened seven stores and closed five, bringing the total to 412 directly operated stores as of September 2026.

The company also addressed its developing relationship with Frasers Group, which now has a 6% stake in the British brand. In October, Frasers Group had adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4%. This came after the growing retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% earlier in the month, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. “We have a long-standing valued relationship with Frasers,” said Schulman. “They are an important wholesale customer for us in the United Kingdom, and now they are an investor. And just like we do with all of our investors, we will meet with Frasers Group in due course. In terms of their agenda, that would be a question for them.”

#6733. The Great Bear Rainforest: How Fashion Rallied to Stop the Deforestation of an Ancient Rainforest

This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa. Read more here.

The Great Bear Rainforest, spanning 6.4 million hectares from the Alaskan border to just above Vancouver Island, is the largest coastal temperate rainforest in the world, a critical carbon sink, and the only known home of the extremely rare white-furred spirit bear. Whales migrate through the rainforest year-round, and it is a major breeding ground for all five species of Pacific salmon. Thanks to the region’s heavy rainfall and nutrient-rich ecosystem, it also houses an array of ancient trees over a thousand years old, including sitka spruce (among the tallest trees in the world) and red western cedar (which hold deep cultural significance for the 26 local First Nations).

Until 2016, 90% of the Great Bear Rainforest was open for logging, and fashion was one of the industries profiting from it. The industry uses large quantities of man-made cellulosic fibers (MMCF) like viscose, modal and lyocell, which typically come from wood pulp. It also has a direct link to deforestation through wood-based packaging, and an indirect link through leather and cotton, which are often grown on deforested land.

Now, thanks to fashion brands joining anti-logging campaigners at a crucial moment, 85% of it is legally protected from deforestation and logging, the First Nations whose territories overlap with it are co-decision makers in its conservation, and there is a $120 million fund helping them transition to conservation-based economies. This is a rare example of fashion rallying around nature restoration and using its purchasing power for good, in partnership with other industries. Experts say it’s a blueprint the industry could apply elsewhere.

This “seismic” win took decades to achieve, says Nicole Rycroft, founder and executive director of non-profit Canopy, which works to conserve ancient and endangered forests around the world. While anti-logging efforts in the Great Bear Rainforest pre-date Canopy, the non-profit joined the campaign at a critical junction, leveraging fashion industry partners including H&M and Zara, to secure the groundbreaking land use agreement when momentum was slowing. “Canopy was one of several organizations that started working with international corporate customers of forest products coming out of that region to send a very clear signal that we don’t want to be sourcing from clear cuts of massive, ecologically critical, temperate rainforests, and we don’t want to be sourcing from spirit bear habitat,” she explains.

A decade on, Vogue Business invited Rycroft to reflect on what the Great Bear Rainforest can teach fashion about nature conservation, and using its purchasing power for good.

Logging happens at the beginning of the supply chain, several steps upstream from where brand traceability programs tend to stop. With such a complex, sprawling supply chain, and such a small number of brands on the hook to comply with traceability regulations, few brands have visibility beyond Tier 1 (garment manufacturing) or Tier 2 (fabric production). Logging would come under Tier 4. That’s why meaningful action starts with traceability, says Rycroft, so brands can understand where their deforestation risks are.

But brands don’t need a direct link to deforestation to make a difference in conservation campaigns. “Even if it’s not a direct or immediate sourcing link, the adjacency is really relevant,” says Rycroft. “Brands are still seen as important even if they’re not existing customers, because there is the potential for them to be future customers.”

Anti-logging efforts in the Great Bear Rainforest started in earnest in the mid-1990s, with conservation organizations standing shoulder to shoulder with local First Nations. But the forestry industry was powerful, so media coverage was largely limited to British Columbia, framing the conflict as a domestic “war in the woods” and failing to break through on the international stage. The turning point came when international brands began sending clear signals to the forestry industry that they did not want to source from ancient and endangered ecosystems. This included home improvement companies such as Home Depot and Lowe’s, as well as major retailers like Sainsbury’s.

But even after the various parties agreed to work toward a land use agreement, progress ebbed and flowed. It took more than a decade to reach a legal agreement, during which time brands and conservations continually applied pressure to keep negotiations on track. “It took consumer companies making phone calls and writing letters to individual forestry companies,” says Rycroft. Fashion joined in later. “The process was long and arduous, and for a long time, there was a blindspot around fashion’s footprint in the Great Bear Rainforest.”

It was Canopy that rallied the fashion industry to get involved. In 2013, it created Canopy Style, an initiative where leading fashion brands commit to end sourcing from ancient and endangered forests. One of the early adopters was Stella McCartney. Within a few months of signing onto the pledge, McCartney canceled her contract with a dissolving pulp mill on Vancouver Island, which was sourcing directly from the Great Bear Rainforest, Canopy discovered. “It sent a very clear signal that fashion is a force to be reckoned with,” says Rycroft.

Later down the line, around 2016, progress stalled again. The land use agreement was 18 months overdue, and even the most ardent supporters were starting to feel stuck. Canopy teamed up with national newspaper The Globe and Mail to host a customer-investor roundtable. The date was set for a month ahead. They invited leading politicians, the forest industry and the First Nations leaders that had been involved in the negotiating process, as well as conservation partners and 70 people representing 70 international brands, including Stella McCartney, Eileen Fisher, H&M, and Zara. “Within days of issuing the invitation, the spirit and intent at the negotiating table changed,” says Rycroft. Twenty-four hours before the roundtable was due to take place, the British Columbia government announced the draft land use agreement.

“Brands have incredible social capital and influence, in addition to being an important economic sector,” says Rycroft. “They can’t be afraid to lean in and flex that muscle.”

Brands that sign up to Canopy Style — or Canopy’s equivalent packaging initiative, Pack4Good — commit to stop sourcing from ancient and endangered forests. That’s the baseline, says Rycroft, the Great Bear Rainforest case study shows that fashion’s nature strategies need to go one step further. They also need to include scaling next-gen and circular alternatives that can ease the industry’s burden on nature, and the risk that burden poses to supply chain resilience.

“Next-gen and circular alternatives are the off-ramp from deforestation and forest degradation,” explains Rycroft. “Brands will not be able to eliminate — or even substantially mitigate — their risk of sourcing from high-carbon, high-biodiversity forests unless we have scaled alternatives.”

At last month’s Textile Exchange conference, Canopy walked the industry through Next Gen Warp Speed, its new initiative that makes the business case for brands to convert 5% of their MMCF basket to next-gen alternatives by 2028. Fashion’s struggle to scale next-gen materials has been well-documented, but Canopy is hoping that a 5% commitment is enough to tip the balance without putting a substantial burden on brands to fund the transition. “A big focus for us now is: how do we create the right conditions and pre-competitive vehicles to scale next-gen production?” says Rycroft.

Moving forward, Canopy is applying its learnings from the Great Bear Rainforest win to other critical ecosystems around the world. Top of its list are the Amazon rainforest and the Leuser Ecosystem in Indonesia, where it already has brand buy-in from the likes of Eileen Fisher and Stella McCartney. Rycroft says she is hopeful that fashion can make a significant difference in these landscapes, just as it did in British Columbia.

A few weeks ago, Rycroft traveled up to the Great Bear Rainforest to see the ecosystem Canopy had worked for so many years to protect. She sat on a riverbank and watched a spirit bear pick salmon out of the stream. “So many people dedicated their lives to this cause, or made a call at a critical juncture, to enable that to happen. It has made such a dramatic difference to the landscape. And now the Great Bear Rainforest truly is a landscape of hope.”

#6730. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6726. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6724. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6722. Ariana Grande Brings Her Two Great Loves—Ricky Álvarez and Rare Vintage—to the Red Carpet

Ariana Grande brought two of her greatest loves to the red carpet last night: boyfriend Ricky Álvarez and a very, very good piece of vintage.

At the New York premiere of Focker-in-Law, the singer and actor made her first red carpet appearance with Álvarez since rekindling their romance earlier this year. And if their constant embraces, adoring glances, and kisses were anything to go by, the pair are very much still in the honeymoon phase.

Stylist Law Roach selected a vintage 1990s Badgley Mischka gown for the occasion. The delicate, spaghetti-strapped design featured a pale silver-gray windowpane check, a fitted bodice scattered with tiny beaded flowers, and a voluminous floor-skimming skirt. She accessorized with Swarovski Matrix hoop earrings—a recent favorite—and traded the flipped bob she’s been sporting of late for a sleek micro ponytail, tied with a little ivory ribbon. Makeup was also her go-to style of glowy and highlight-dominant.

Roach is on a particularly impressive archival streak of late. He’s been mining the fashion vaults for Kim Kardashian’s All's Fair press tour, pulling everything from 1990s Dolce & Gabbana to Paco Rabanne couture. Just last weekend, he dressed Anya Taylor-Joy in a spectacularly ruffled spring 1997 Pierre Cardin ensemble for the LACMA Art+Film Gala.

Grande has long been a devotee of fashion’s more whimsical, romantic history. Her love of vintage reached particularly fanciful heights during the Wicked press tours, but the singer has since held firmly to her soft, ultra-feminine aesthetic with 1950s silhouettes and diaphanous fabrics. At one point, her dedication to the look was so pronounced that some wondered whether she was quietly auditioning for a rumored Audrey Hepburn biopic. Roach revealed that he’d bought the Badgley Mischka gown months earlier, drawn to its connection with the era of the original Meet the Parents film.

Álvarez, for his part, kept things considerably more low-key. The dancer and photographer wore a relaxed black blazer over an open-neck white shirt, tucked into dark indigo jeans with rolled cuffs, a leather belt, and brown shoes. Some classic easy-going boyfriend dressing. He spent much of the evening with an arm around Grande’s waist, while she leaned into him, held his hands, and beamed up at him for the cameras.

Of course, the couple’s love story has its own history. Grande and Álvarez first met when he worked as a backup dancer on her Honeymoon Tour in 2015. They dated for around a year before splitting in 2016, and he later received a memorable name-check in her 2018 breakup anthem, “thank u, next.” Almost a decade later, however, things have come full circle. Rumors of a reunion began circulating this summer when the pair were spotted together in Austin, Texas, during Grande’s Eternal Sunshine tour, before more sightings followed in Florida and New York. By August, they were Instagram official, and Grande had debuted a new tattoo reading “I do love you”, seemingly matching a similar inscription on Álvarez’s collarbone. The two were also spotted arm-in-arm around London, where Grande completed her 10-night residency at the O2. She even began rewriting the Ricky lyrics in “thank u, next” onstage. At one Brooklyn show, she sang, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / We always find our way back.” By the tour’s September finale in London, the sentiment had become considerably more definitive: “I’m tryna make him my last.”

More recently, they’ve been enjoying some more ordinary couple activities, including cheering on runners at the New York City Marathon earlier this month. Grande has also enlisted Álvarez for a particularly kiss-heavy R.E.M. Beauty lip-product guessing game on Instagram. The adoration and affection is showing no signs of slowing down.

Between a decade-old romance finding new life and a beautiful dress pulled from the archives, Ariana Grande is making a persuasive case for revisiting the past.

#6721. The Mysterious Fridge Hacks Hitting Grocery Stores

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the Cheesecake Factory culture war.

Death, taxes, and Martha Stewart doing something weird online every six to eight weeks: These are the constants in our ever-chaotic lives. This round involved a quickly deleted Instagram post showing Stewart apparently dressed as a homeless person—she was holding a clipboard (?) with a message in marker that read “I am hungry help me!!”

She released a series of statements apologizing for the gaffe, and at one point seemed to blame Today show host Craig Melvin, who, she said, spilled chocolate on the sweater she’d planned on wearing to a costume party later that night, forcing her to improvise a new costume on the fly.

But enough of Martha! We have more important things to worry about.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the mysterious refrigeration system hacks plaguing Europe, DC's newly minted foie gras ban, the GLP-1 gap relationship, and a democratic victory is celebrated at a Whataburger, naturally.

Dozens of supermarkets across seven countries were the victims of hacking that took control of their refrigeration systems this week. The hackers shifted grocery freezers into defrost mode, the freezers began blowing hot air onto the frozen food, and, in some, temperatures rose to 122 degrees. Needless to say a lot of food was deemed spoiled and had to be thrown out.

Three weeks ago, similar attacks hit grocery stores in France. It was the same story: defrost mode, hot air, lots of wasted food and money. Officials are investigating who may be responsible, but so far the culprits and their motives remain a mystery. The BBC reports that experts believe hackers in Russia or Iran—or simply teenagers playing a prank—could be responsible.

Could something like this happen in the US? Well, it sort of already has. In August six military bases across the country reported some odd refrigeration malfunctions—the same kind we’ve been seeing in Europe. The Pentagon is investigating the incident as a suspected hack, but that’s about as much information as we can glean.

The FBI on Thursday issued a warning about “malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems around the world.”

As Democrats celebrated a resounding wave of victories in this week’s midterm elections, so too did duck and goose lovers. Washington, DC, voted to approve a ballot measure banning the sale and production of foie gras. It was a controversial issue in the area, as I covered in last week’s Open Tab video, which saw big name chefs come forward to defend the making, selling, and eating of foie gras. The discourse got heated, topical Halloween costumes abounded.

The ban will go into effect July 1, 2027, so foie-heads have some time to get their fill. But it’s not that simple. A New York foie gras company has said it will take legal action against the ban, calling it “unconstitutional on several grounds." To put the ban in effect would face further logistical barriers too. DC’s chief financial officer has estimated it would cost more than $300,000 over four fiscal years to implement it—money that’s not currently allocated in the budget.

Despite the upcoming ban, Bart Hutchins, chef and co-owner of Butterworth’s who was one of the ban’s most vocal opponents, has said he’ll continue serving foie gras in his restaurants. “I will still be serving it for another decade,” he told the Washington Post.

What happens when one partner gets on a GLP-1 and the other partner doesn’t? We know that GLP-1’s can shift your sex drive, and that they can have an effect on your mental health, but often, it seems, there’s anecdotal evidence that they can have a profound effect on your relationships. A report in the Washington Post details how, for some couples, starting a GLP-1 can disrupt a couple's routines and equilibrium—deciding on a date night restaurant, for instance—which can create divisions. There simply isn’t enough data to measure how GLP-1’s might be linked to divorce rates, but some experts point to statistics attached to bariatric surgeries, another weight loss intervention, which found that married couples are twice as likely to get divorced after getting the procedure.

Midterm elections in the US brought a number of historic firsts, including the first Muslim senator (Michigan), the first openly gay man senator (New Hampshire), and the first Black woman governor (Georgia). Notably, voters managed to flip Texas, turning the state blue for the first time in decades.

How did Texas Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa celebrate their wins? At a Whataburger. It’s a surprisingly poignant statement about the affordability politics that was foundational to many Democratic wins this election cycle. Read on to learn more.

#6720. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6718. Kim Kardashian Plays Nurse in One of Louis Vuitton’s Rarest Runway Looks

Kim Kardashian has been raiding the fashion archives with extraordinary enthusiasm of late, but her latest vintage pull comes with a health warning. Enter: a very rare, almost 20-year-old Louis Vuitton nurse uniform, complete with a monogrammed lace face mask, personalized cap, and coordinating accessories. The look, from Marc Jacobs’s spring 2008 collection for the house, is a heart-palpitating piece of runway history.

The ensemble was sourced by stylist Law Roach from the personal archive of Lauren Pyes, a Boston-based Harvard University employee and avid collector of Jacobs-era Louis Vuitton, whose extraordinary collection Vogue first explored last year. Pyes has spent years scouring resale platforms, boutiques, and obscure corners of the internet for some of the designer’s most coveted creations, amassing what she affectionately calls the “Marchive.”

“Law reached out to me a few months ago and was interested in pieces of the Marchive," Pyes tells Vogue. “Suffice to say, I was thrilled to loan them to him.” When Roach first contacted her, she could scarcely believe it was him. “I kept toggling back and forth to make sure it wasn’t a spam account!” she recalls. “Although he has a larger-than-life public persona, Law is deeply kind and gracious in addition to being the visionary he is rightly lauded as. I have so much respect for his dedication to telling stories through fashion and his commitment to finding the pieces that do exactly that.”

And few collections have quite as much storytelling potential as Louis Vuitton’s spring 2008 offering. Presented in Paris in October 2007, the show opened with a procession of supermodels—including Naomi Campbell, Stephanie Seymour, Eva Herzigova, and Nadja Auermann—dressed as nurses in sheer, pastel-colored uniforms, black lace masks, and white caps. The inspiration was the American artist Richard Prince, whose provocative Nurse Paintings informed the collection and accompanying collaboration with the house. Reviewing the collection at the time, Vogue’s Sarah Mower described it as a “typical Jacobs coup of multidimensional, referential, and self-referential significance,” and a “hilariously kinky parade” that “reflected Jacobs’s way of walking the line between creative freedom and commercial innovation.” It was one of Jacobs’s most deviant, deliciously strange runway spectacles.

The shoes from Louis Vuitton spring 2028.

The full look, as sourced by Lauren Pyes.

Kim Kardashian’s interpretation was remarkably faithful to the original. She wore the sheer, short-sleeved white nurse’s coat cinched at the waist over a delicate, peach-colored silk dress, with white stockings and peep-toe heels. A black lace Louis Vuitton face mask covered her mouth, while a white nurse’s cap (commissioned by Roach and reimagined by legendary milliner Stephen Jones) bearing a red “K” sat atop her sleek dark hair. In her arms was another treasure from the collection: an Aquarelle Papillon bag. The shoes also hailed from spring 2008.

Bringing together such a complete ensemble was no small undertaking. “I sourced these pieces from all over—including platforms like Poshmark and Vestiaire Collective—for over a year,” Pyes explains. The dresses have become a particular obsession: she has owned four, including a pink silk satin version that remains in her permanent collection. Vogue actually purchased another of the orange dresses—the same color Kardashian wore—from Pyes a little over a year ago. But the real rarity is the mask and overcoat, which Pyes considers among her most treasured finds. Earlier this year, the ensemble was exhibited at the Savannah College of Art and Design (SCAD), where it even caught the attention of one of its original creators.

“I had it exhibited at SCAD back in April, and Stephen Jones—who made it in collaboration with Louis Vuitton—was apparently surprised that it even existed!” Pyes says of the mask. “If the person who made it was in disbelief by seeing it, I guess that means it is pretty rare!”

Kardashian and Roach have been on a formidable archival streak throughout the All’s Fair press tour, resurrecting everything from ’90s Paco Rabanne couture to vintage Dolce & Gabbana and Jean Paul Gaultier-era Hermès. The Louis Vuitton nurse look is their most playful fashion deep dive yet.

And for Pyes, it’s precisely that irreverence that makes the Jacobs years so compelling. She points to the extraordinary creative team behind the collection, including Peter Copping, then head of womenswear and now creative director of Lanvin, and Camille Miceli, currently at the helm of Pucci. “This collection and these pieces are so special because they highlight what Marc and his team did so well—seamlessly integrating fashion and art into a cohesive and powerful narrative,” she says. She remembers the supermodel casting, the nurse uniforms, and even Jacobs taking his final bow beside a custom Vuitton trunk playing an episode of SpongeBob SquarePants. “There are so many elements that were unexpected and genuine in a pre-social media age.”

Pyes, of course, has continued to do some killer sourcing. She’s recently completed a “trifecta of accessories” from the Louis Vuitton fall 2011 collection, better known as the “Fetish Collection.” This includes a shearling porter hat, mask hair accessory, and a patent leather bib. On the non-vintage side of things? “I am champing at the bit to receive the custom order I put in from Marc’s Spring 2027 collection,” she shares. “After more than 40 years, he continues to create incredible fashion and I feel fortunate to be adding this ensemble to the Marchive!”

Whether Kim’s look was a Halloween latergram, another cheeky press tour outing, or just a moment of play inside an impressive archive, for now, is anyone’s guess. Whatever the occasion, Pyes is delighted to see the collection enjoying a new life in the public imagination. Nearly two decades after its debut, Jacobs’s peculiar, provocative vision remains as potent as ever. “These clothes are not just beautiful and special,” she says, “but also consequential. This collection walked almost 20 years ago and yet continues to figure so largely in pop culture and the imagination of fashion lovers.” Nurse Kardashia, the defibrillator please!

#6716. 53 Healthy Thanksgiving Recipes to Brighten Up the Table

What makes a healthy Thanksgiving recipe? To us, it’s less about cutting out butter or skipping pie and more about bringing balance to the table. Crisp, bitter greens make creamy mashed potatoes taste even better. Tart cranberries cut through rich turkey gravy. Beans, whole grains, and plenty of colorful vegetables bring flavor, texture, and variety to a meal that can otherwise skew decidedly beige.

These healthy Thanksgiving recipes cover the entire feast, from crunchy salads and make-ahead appetizers to satisfying plant-forward mains and festive desserts. Some offer more fiber or protein; others give seasonal produce a starring role. What they have in common is that every one is delicious. You’ll also find plenty of vegan, gluten-free, and dairy-free options too. Because there’s room for everyone—and everything—at the Thanksgiving table.

Deep purple cabbage, bitter radicchio, juicy citrus, and ruby-red pomegranate seeds make a strong case for putting salad front and center. Give the cabbage a good massage to soften it without sacrificing its crunch.

“In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake,” writes Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser. Here, thinly sliced pears get a shower of honey-roasted seeds and shaved cheese.

Instead of tender greens that might wilt before everyone sits down, consider a fennel salad that stays crunchy for hours. Walnuts, Parmesan, croutons, and lemon give it plenty of flavor and texture.

Who says salad has to be cold? Caramelized cauliflower, warm feta, crunchy pistachios, and sticky dates meet peppery arugula and a tangy vinaigrette. Hearty enough to satisfy, with plenty of greens to keep things fresh.

Bitter radicchio meets sweet apple and mustardy croutons in this hearty autumn salad. Tossing the apple slices with cider vinegar helps keep them from browning before the feast begins.

A Thanksgiving salad should be sturdy enough to hold its own on the buffet table. This one only gets better after it’s dressed, as the kale softens and the nutty pecan vinaigrette works its way into the leaves.

Cranberry sauce isn’t just for turkey. A tart dressing made with the canned stuff brings holiday spirit to bitter greens, sweetened pecans, and Manchego cheese. Consider it a little insurance against salad fatigue.

Warm spices and sweet carrots give this hearty lentil salad plenty of character. The legumes add plant-based protein and fiber, making it a substantial addition to a vegetarian Thanksgiving spread.

Panzanella isn’t just for summer. Swap ripe tomatoes for juicy oranges, add bitter chicories and shaved fennel, and toss everything with toasted pumpernickel croutons and a balsamic-Dijon vinaigrette.

Roasted carrots, chickpeas, almonds, and smoked paprika blend into a vibrant dip with a little protein and plenty of personality. Make it up to a week ahead, then serve with seeded crackers, crudités, or good bread.

Another excellent addition to the crudité platter. Hazelnuts bring out the earthy sweetness of beets, while garlic and lemon keep everything lively. Like the carrot dip above, this one can be made a week ahead.

A jar of olives, a block of feta, and some garlicky olive oil: That’s nearly all you need for this bright, briny appetizer. Have some crusty bread handy for the flavorful oil left in the bowl.

Yuzu kosho gives these deviled eggs a jolt of citrusy heat, while pickled shallots, fresh herbs, and thinly sliced radishes bring brightness and crunch. Arrange them on shiso leaves for an especially striking holiday appetizer.

A bowl of party nuts is never a bad idea, particularly when they’re seasoned with chile powder, fried curry leaves, and crispy onions. Set these out while the turkey finishes roasting.

A tangy, Parmesan-rich dressing clings to crisp-tender green beans, with pickled shallots bringing a sharp little kick. All the satisfaction of a proper Thanksgiving side, without the casserole dish.

Crispy onions are the crown on this roasted squash side; pomegranate seeds are the jewels. Add fresh herbs and a swoop of lemony yogurt, and you’ve got a dish worthy of the center of the table.

These collards aren’t cooked into submission. Simmered until just tender, they stay pleasantly substantial beneath a sharp mustard vinaigrette. Tarragon and sweet-salty walnuts finish this fresh take on a holiday greens side.

When the oven is too crowded for green bean casserole, make this stovetop alternative. Browned mushrooms, crisp-tender green beans, butter, and frizzled shallots deliver plenty of familiar holiday flavor.

One BA reader calls this their signature Thanksgiving sprouts recipe. Separating the individual leaves takes patience, but the payoff is worth it: tender-crisp greens with lots of caramelized edges.

Toss sprouts with spicy, nutty gochujang brown butter. Or, for something simpler, go for classic roasted brussels sprouts.

Coconut milk gives this bubbling, breadcrumb-topped vegan gratin its creamy consistency without any dairy. A little lemon zest and nutmeg round things out.

White miso gives these glazed carrots a deep savoriness, while scallion gremolata adds freshness. You can cook the carrots a day ahead and loosen the glaze with a splash of water when reheating.

Maple syrup plays up carrots’ natural sweetness, while a pinch of chile flakes keeps the glaze from going full candy. This is a classic Thanksgiving side with just enough heat to keep things interesting.

Or skip cooking the carrots altogether. Shave them into thin ribbons, let salt soften them slightly, then toss with sticky dates and an orange vinaigrette. Sweet, tart, crunchy, and fresh.

Blanch, smash, and dress the beans up to 12 hours ahead so they can soak up the lemony sumac vinaigrette. Finish with Asian pear, parsley, and crunchy pumpkin seeds just before serving.

Silken tofu gives this steakhouse classic its creamy texture without dairy. Aromatics add savory depth, making it a satisfying side to serve alongside turkey, stuffing, and potatoes.

Bitter greens, tangy heat, and salty crunch are especially welcome among Thanksgiving’s softer sides. Toss tender broccoli rabe with garlicky onions and pickled cherry peppers, then shower the lot with crisp Pecorino breadcrumbs.

The French bistro classic gets a holiday-friendly update: Cut the leeks into rounds rather than long stalks, making them easier to serve to a crowd. A sharp vinaigrette, toasted walnuts, and fresh tarragon finish the dish.

Steamed broccolini gets a salty-sweet dressing of tahini, miso, soy sauce, and mirin, then a scattering of lemon and sesame seeds. Make the sauce a day ahead to take one more task off your Thanksgiving list.

Sweet roasted beets meet tart grapefruit, sharp shallots, and sizzling rosemary. The colors alone could wake up a Thanksgiving spread. Plus, you can roast and peel the beets up to two days ahead.

Inspired by Cantonese steamed fish, this squash side gets a generous pouf of frizzled scallions. Ginger and chile bring the heat, turning a humble vegetable into something special.

Bharta is a Bangladeshi preparation of seasoned meat or mashed vegetables. This roasted squash version gets its punch from mustard oil, chiles, spices, and fresh cilantro.

Raw cranberries keep their tart snap in this bright relish, while toasted walnuts, mustard seeds, Fresno chile, and a little maple syrup bring crunch, heat, and sweetness. Make it up to four days ahead.

A quick parboil and a vigorous shake rough up the surfaces of these potatoes, helping them develop exceptionally crunchy crusts in the oven. The fluffy centers are practically made for soaking up gravy.

Baking potatoes instead of boiling them concentrates their flavor, while roasted garlic adds savory depth. With just six tablespoons of butter for four pounds of potatoes, this creamy mash is a little less indulgent than many holiday versions.

Steaming sweet potatoes makes their flesh especially soft and fluffy, ready for generous smears of tahini butter. Lime juice, soy sauce, and sesame oil make the flavors especially dynamic, and a welcome savory counterpoint to classic sweet potato casserole.

Thin rounds of sweet potato are arranged upright in concentric circles, then roasted with harissa until tender and crisp-edged. A crunchy dukkah of pistachios, sesame, and fennel seeds finishes this striking holiday side.

This gluten-free stuffing skips the usual process of baking cornbread, cubing it, and drying it out. Instead, mushrooms, kale, and herbs bake right into the batter.

Chewy wild rice, tossed with sautéed leeks, toasted pecans, and fresh herbs, makes a stunningly delicious (and gluten-free) alternative to traditional Thanksgiving stuffing.

If you’re firmly Team Dark Meat, these stock-braised turkey legs are the ticket. The meat becomes tender enough to pull from the bone, making for especially good leftover sandwiches the next day.

Prefer white meat, or feeding a smaller crowd? A bone-in turkey breast delivers juicy, flavorful slices without the work of roasting a whole bird. No basting or oversized roasting pan required.

Or give a whole roasted salmon fillet the holiday treatment with a crunchy salsa of toasted nuts, garlic, chile, and vinegar. Showered with fresh mint and cilantro, it’s a striking centerpiece with plenty of protein.

A crisp, golden shell of saffron rice gives way to spiced chickpeas, caramelized onions, and tart dried cherries. Crown the whole thing with a bracingly fresh herb salad for a vegetarian centerpiece everyone will love.

For a meatless main with all the ceremony of a holiday roast, this homemade tofu loaf gets filled with savory mushroom-pecan stuffing and brushed with a smoky maple-soy glaze. Pass the mushroom gravy alongside.

Tearing roasted sweet potatoes into rough chunks creates more surface area for charring and catching a spicy maple-soy glaze. Serve them over tangy lentils with scallions and pistachios for a substantial plant-based main.

A mixture of mushrooms, pearl onions, carrots, and red wine makes a rich, deeply savory vegetarian braise. Serve it over mashed potatoes or polenta, with crispy mushrooms scattered over the top.

Transform humble cabbage into a deeply flavorful vegetarian centerpiece. Here, it caramelizes while slowly braising in a spiced tomato broth. Serve the tender wedges over grains to make the meal more substantial.

Almond flour makes these warmly spiced cake layers exceptionally tender, while shredded carrots, walnuts, golden raisins, and coconut bring texture to every bite. Tangy cream cheese–Greek yogurt frosting seals the deal. Make it up to three days ahead.

Whole wheat flour and oats bring subtle nuttiness to this apple crisp, while brown sugar and butter help the topping turn golden. Serve warm, with vanilla ice cream for anyone who wants it.

This Spanish almond cake gets a seasonal turn with chopped pears and plenty of citrus zest. Naturally gluten-free and dairy-free, it’s lovely after dinner—and just as welcome with coffee the next morning.

Rich chocolate mousse gets a crackly crown of sweet sesame brittle. Serve it in individual glasses for a holiday-party-worthy capper that’s entirely vegan—and a little different from the usual parade of Thanksgiving desserts.

Golden turmeric, fragrant spices, and coconut milk give this custard pie its silky filling. The almond, oat, and coconut crust is naturally gluten-free, making the finished dessert suitable for guests avoiding both gluten and dairy.

A platter of seasonal citrus—think grapefruit, mandarin oranges, and whatever else looks good at the market—gets a crunchy topping of pistachios, almonds, pumpkin seeds, and toasted coconut.

#6715. Past and Prologue: Burberry’s Daniel Lee is Bringing Fashion—and His Extended Family—Home.

Daniel Lee must be considering the notion of home a lot these days. Not just his 17th-century country house in his native Yorkshire, which he bought last year, but his London place, on a leafy 19th-century square, where he has lived for the last five years. Lee, Burberry’s chief creative officer, is enjoying a reprieve from having repair professionals in—the AC has been on the blink, the underfloor heating went awry, and he has already endured one soul-destroying flood. On this hot July morning, he has sequestered himself in the basement, decorated with a beige sectional sofa and a Gary Hume painting, Greenness Is a Kind of Grief. The room looks onto the garden, and Lee has taken to lying out on a lounger; by adjusting its angle and that of the television, he can watch soccer from outside.

“My social life is watching the match on TV; it’s a bit sad, isn’t it?” Lee says in a soft voice accented by dry humor. “I love all sport—Wimbledon’s great—but I prefer the energy of a football match to a tennis match. Tennis is very polite. People lose themselves at football—it’s like a cult, isn’t it?” I didn’t have Lee down as a sports fanatic, but he seems to revere footballers as much as the likes of Skepta and Olivia Colman, whom he loves collaborating with. (Lee supports Arsenal.) There’s also his daily 8 a.m. gym sessions before work. “The bench press is nice, because you can just lie there,” he says, laughing. “I don’t love cardio anymore—it hurts my knees.”

From left: Edie Campbell wears silk poplin trench coat and sequined georgette dress. Alva Claire wears map-print nylon sateen trench coat. Clothes and accessories (throughout), Burberry.

Lee, 40, tells me this as we sit in his garden, the first of our several meetings. In person, Lee is candid, funny, and thoughtful. “Daniel appreciates realness—and openness,” says Skepta. “And he has the best eye. I’d pretty much wear everything he makes.”

Appointed Burberry’s chief creative officer in 2022, Lee has taken the 170-year-old British brand from his highly conceptual debut, all electric-blue blanket checks and graphic red-rose prints, to his more recent collections, widely praised as much for their cool, considered functionality as for the cut and thrust of their forward direction. (Lee has also seen the brand reach pretax profits of over $65 million in 2026, up from an almost $88 million loss last year.) He came to Burberry after three years at Bottega Veneta—an era that flared up like a firework thanks to the success of the Cassette bag and Lido sandals, with Lee quitting before the spark extinguished itself. Before that: six years with Phoebe Philo at Celine, eventually becoming her design director; and before that Donna Karan in New York, following internships at Maison Margiela and Nicolas Ghesquière–era Balenciaga after his graduation from Central Saint Martins.

While the CV reads like a conceptualist designer’s dream, Lee’s Burberry role may be the most reflective of who he really is: pragmatic, unpretentious, driven by a sense of purpose. For his friend Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, who has known him since Bottega Veneta, Lee the person and the designer are one and the same. “The reason I feel so at ease in Daniel’s company is that he is grounded and down-to-earth,” she says. “He has this incredible talent and work ethic, yet there’s no pretense with him, no drama.”

From left: Romeo Beckham wears silk shirt, silk scarf, leather trousers, belt, and biker boots. Simone Ashley wears embellished satin dress, leather shoes, and frame bag. Paapa Essiedu wears nylon sateen trench coat, silk shirt, wool trousers, and leather shoes.

When he started at Burberry, Lee says, “it took me a minute to adjust. What I did in the past was about the dream [of fashion], and it was the accessories that were the focus. The clothes here are still the dream, yet they’re wearable and useful, not just for a show. Designing Burberry makes you question and consider everything.” He sees himself as “a making designer,” he says. “I enjoy being in the moment and working with instinct, with craft, with my hands—the physicality of that.”

Lee’s love of making comes from his family—his father Ian and mother Jenny, his brother Richard and sister Sophie. (Daniel is the eldest.) Ian was a mechanic before he retired, and he now lives in Lee’s Yorkshire home, which is not far from Bradford, where Lee was born and raised. He’s set up a workshop at the back of the house to renovate motorcycles, a lifelong passion, which delights his son to no end—when he and his brother were kids, they would ride the bikes in a field at the back of their house. His mom was the creative one. “She was always making—sewing curtains and baking fancy birthday cakes; she made a Noah’s ark for us, and she even made my aunt, who had a cleaning business, a vacuum cleaner,” Lee says. “It made me think, I just want a job where I can make things.”

Simone wears leather shirt, pleated leather skirt, boots, and bag.

Curtains that Lee’s mom sewed for the family living room now hang in one of the bedrooms at his house in Yorkshire, although “his” is a bit of a misnomer: Lee sees the place as his whole family’s home. The impetus to find somewhere in the area came in the aftermath of his mom’s death just before Christmas 2024. “In those moments,” Lee says, “the creative element of work was soothing—it was like therapy.” He hadn’t even been thinking about getting a place up north, but the undertow of emotion carried him there. His brother and sister-in-law, who live locally, were looking to buy a new home. Lee joined the hunt, and the house he ended up taking was the first and only one he saw. “Before that, I’d always had this quest to live abroad, work abroad, see the world,” he says. “When you’re young, you feel like you’ve got endless time—[then] you realize that, actually, time is finite. My family’s not going to be around forever. I want to spend more time with them.” (One area where Lee would rather keep his private life private is when it comes to dating, though he readily says that he’d like to start his own family: “I would love to have children.”)

His aunt Debbie, his mom’s sister, has moved next door to the 1680s house. It was Debbie who brought Lee to London for the first time when he was 12—they saw the London Eye, took in The Lion King, and ate at the then hip restaurant Sketch. “My aunt was being trendy,” Lee says, laughing affectionately. “She also took me to Harvey Nichols in Leeds. I wasn’t a kid growing up reading Vogue, but looking at the amazing windows at Harvey Nichols and seeing the clothes—that’s when I started to think about fashion.” His grandparents would take him to the Alhambra Theatre in Bradford to see the likes of Chicago (his grandmother’s favorite), which ignited a lifelong love of theater. (On a recent trip to New York, he caught the much-lauded revival of The Rocky Horror Show.)

While Lee’s family has always attended his Burberry runway shows, in the weeks and months after his mom’s death, the closeness deepened. His grandmother came to the show in February 2025 with a photograph of Lee’s mom in her handbag, and it was she who sat with him the night before the presentation as he worked on the last of the fittings. His sister, meanwhile, wore the Bur­berry trench that had been their mom’s. “She wore it to my first show,” Lee recalls.

“One thing about Daniel is that he has never forgotten his roots,” says Lee’s father, “and I think that’s why Yorkshire will always feel like home to him.” That feeling of reconnection is something to which Lee has given a lot of thought. “That’s the real value of the North [for me],” he says. “It gives you a sense of shared ownership of the difficult times, which makes things easier.”

Burberry’s headquarters are on Horseferry Road in London, walking distance from both Buckingham Palace and Tate Britain. Lee’s office and studio are on the seventh floor. He designs Tuesday to Thursday, reserving Monday and Friday for prep days—so the team, he says, can have their weekends free of work. Lee likes to be efficient—the late Virgil Abloh told him that creative directors shouldn’t waste their time emailing, so he doesn’t: He and his team speak constantly via WhatsApp instead.

In one corner of the vast workroom, Burberry archivist Carly Eck has assembled a rail of pieces taken from the 25,000 that the company holds—including the earliest trench, dating from 1917—with an eye to what Lee has responded to: the 1930s Highlander cape, with straps to allow freedom of movement; a motoring overall that Lee riffed on for his fall 2024 collection; and a coat worn by explorer Ernest Shackleton, which Lee also referenced in 2023. Eck and Lee get together at the beginning of every season to help build narratives connecting Burberry past and present. Lee’s intense curiosity has certainly paid unexpected dividends. The ridiculously cute duck hats that he included in his Burberry debut were inspired by drawings in one of the brand’s catalogs circa 1930s, laid out on a table nearby.

“What we do,” Lee says, “is try to provide people with answers about how to live the best possible way. We make clothes to protect people, to make them feel good, ready, sophisticated. I think the fashion is secondary. The design here starts from a place of utility, functionality, practicality—it has to work before it has to be, let’s say, decorative.” His Burberry collections thus far have variously offered blanket-lined parkas, battalion jackets, long kilts, jaunty capelets, and dandyish suiting; what model and equestrian Edie Campbell, who has worked with Burberry since she was 15 (“I still had braces!”), calls “very wearable, but with an edge. It’s joyful, and there’s a lightness and a playfulness to it.” Accessories—the ka-ching! successes for any fashion brand—are on his mind, even if a star hasn’t quite emerged yet.

But if the past is in the room, so is the future. Burberry’s spring 2027 collection, which he showed in September at Chelsea College of Arts—Jodie Turner-Smith, Jonathan Bailey, and Fiona Shaw on the front row; Central Cee on the catwalk—features trenches both diaphanous and etched with embroidery, as well as rendered in leather that’s been lavishly traced with beading; utilitarian cotton drill mixed with sequins; floral blousons and skirts worn with earthy, low-heeled buckled mules; and jewel-like high slingback shoes made a little less precious by being paired with slouchy socks. One thing always on Lee’s mind: making Burberry speak more to women. “The brand is born out of menswear, and the trenches are a very masculine thing,” he says. “We’re always trying to bring more femininity to it.”

Edie wears silk poplin jacket with shearling trim, sequined jersey dress, and leather shoes.

Color is one way into that, and it’s something that Lee has decisively brought to the brand from the very beginning with what he describes as softer, moorland tones; spring 2027, meanwhile, sings with shades of dusky pink, aubergine, duck-egg blue, and a soft-sunny yellow, reflecting the casual, lived-in feel that he wanted to impart on the clothes. Gary Hume, the painter, recalls meeting Lee when they began working on a Burberry project in 2024. Walking around Hume’s studio, they’d touch the art, communing with it. Having now worked with Lee, the artist feels that the designer’s use of color “doesn’t feel like it’s added on—it’s entirely integral to what Daniel does.”

For spring 2027, Lee also worked with the celebrated octogenarian print designer Celia Birtwell, an intrinsic part of the creative explosion in British art and design in the 1960s, along with her husband, designer Ossie Clark, and David Hockney, her close friend. Lee had gone to see the recent Hockney exhibition at the Serpentine Galleries in London—he feels a strong affinity with the Bradford-born artist, who died in June—and a gingham tablecloth that Hockney used as a leitmotif sparked an idea to collaborate with Birtwell, who created a check with a painterly feel to it and some rather charming vintage-wallpaper floral prints. They feel organic and fresh, a million miles away from CAD—or AI. “Celia brings a human hand, an emotional hand, to something,” Lee says, thrilled by what she has done. “We have an incredible archive, but sometimes it’s exciting to see new things.”

From left: Alva wears mohair/silk shawl coat and chevron-knit dress. Romeo wears leather jacket with shearling collar, silk shirt, flocked jeans, and belt.

Lee and I are to meet for the last time at the Regency Café near the Bur­berry headquarters. Founded in 1946, it hasn’t changed much since, still a haven of egg and chips, Formica, and tea so wonderfully strong you could stand a teaspoon up in it. In its own way, the café’s story isn’t so different from Burberry’s: halcyon Britain, yet a Britishness of global fascination. Seated among the Regency regulars are hordes of creatively dressed kids from all around the world Instagramming their full English breakfasts—the very kind of young, style-conscious types who Burberry would want to attract, though not only them, of course. It is an egalitarian brand, as much for the aristo in a beaten-up trench driving a Land Rover as it is for the bloke on the football terraces.

Pride in Britishness is, after all, intrinsic to Burberry. “It stands for heritage and culture, and all the things and all the people that those mean,” says model Alva Claire, and Lee seconds the thought. “We are the most famous British luxury brand,” he says, “but in a way we’re bigger than fashion: We are a British institution. We’re there to celebrate the best of Britain—great creativity and also great locations.” Lee recounts how so many of his Burberry shoots have been deliberately located outside of London—Skye, Somerset, Norfolk, the Lake District—and he readily agrees (while acknowledging the importance of London Fashion Week to Burberry) that it would be great to show somewhere else in the UK. But where? “Chanel did Manchester…,” I say; “Dior did Scotland,” he adds.

Lee on the winding, cobbled streets of Haworth, in West Yorkshire.

Right now, though, Lee is thinking about 170 years’ worth of moments. The anniversary is, he says, “always on our minds. How do we do it justice? We have been ambitious this year.” Indeed: As well as a monthslong campaign photographing 170 people all over the world wearing Burberry, a special exhibition, “The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon,” is at the V&A ahead of the company’s funding of the museum’s new costume wing, opening in 2028; another Burberry exhibition, “Ever Forward: The Archive On Stage,” opens this month in Shanghai.

Anyone would be asking themselves what’s left to do—and for Lee, there’s plenty. Top of mind for him, professionally, is transforming the brand’s retail environments for its 413 outposts around the world. Personally? Well, he wouldn’t mind, at some point in his life, living in a hot country. Yet he’s not in any rush. He wants progress to be measured and meaningful; to take it in stride. “I mean,” he says, smiling, “I really feel quite content.”

In this story: Hair, Mari Ohashi; makeup, Siobhan Furlong; grooming, Quelle Bester; manicurist, Robbie Tomkins; tailor, Della George.

#6714. Culture Watch: What to See and Where to Go in November

Culture Watch is a series spotlighting the intersection of fashion and art, bringing you the latest must-see exhibitions, pop-ups, installations, and more.

November is a good month to make a little room in your calendar. As the holiday season starts to gather pace, galleries, brands, and creative spaces are offering plenty of reasons to get out and look around. In New York, Salon Art + Design returns for its 15th year, while Loro Piana presents its “Master of Cashmere” installation at The Brant Foundation; farther afield, international exhibitions offer even more to explore. Check out all of this month’s best cultural happenings below.

Louis Vuitton Presents ‘La Valise Bruno Aveillan’ at LV Dream

For 13 years, photographer and filmmaker Bruno Aveillan has taken his Louis Vuitton Alzer suitcase to more than 100 destinations, making it a recurring presence in his work. Now, the well-traveled case is at the center of “La Valise Bruno Aveillan,” an immersive exhibition at LV Dream, the house’s encompassing destination in Paris. Aveillan’s photographs appear alongside historic Louis Vuitton trunks and a closer look at the craftsmanship behind the Alzer, the brand’s hard-sided suitcase built around a sturdy wooden frame. The exhibition marks the final chapter in the house’s yearlong celebration of the monogram’s 130th anniversary.

Loro Piana Names Its Cashmere of the Year and Unveils a ‘Master of Cashmere’ Installation

Loro Piana put cashmere in the spotlight at The Brant Foundation in New York, where it marked the 11th edition of its Cashmere of the Year Award. Established in 2015 and held stateside for the first time, the prize recognizes the herders who produce the finest cashmere fiber. Coinciding with the honor, which went to three couples of cashmere herders from Inner Mongolia, is “Master of Cashmere: The Quest for Fiber Excellence,” an installation that traces the material from its origins to the Maison’s work with it. The multi-room experience features archival sketches, explanatory timelines, and, of course, soft-to-the-touch cashmere.

Salon Art + Design Returns to the Park Avenue Armory for Its 15th Year

The 15th edition of Salon Art + Design is now on view at the Park Avenue Armory—and it’s one of its most immersive, expansive editions yet. As is tradition, the event brings together collectible design, fine art, and jewelry. The event is open through November 8. Standouts include Jean Dunand’s 1929 La Forêt lacquered screen, Michel Dufet’s 1918 daybeds, and Jean Royère’s illuminated desk. Fernando Mastrangelo’s totem lamps add a sculptural note, while the jewelry lineup includes pieces from Fernando Jorge, Mellerio, Cora Sheibani, and Viltier.

Lara Saget Debuts Her First New York Solo Show, ‘And the World Came Apart’

Lara Saget brings more than a decade of material experimentation to her first solo exhibition in New York. At Trotter&Sholer’s new Elizabeth Street space, her sculptures and wearable works fuse glass, stone, and metal through heat, pressure, and time. Drawing on geological processes and NASA data, the show moves from ancient natural formations to humanity’s rapid impact on the planet.

The Phillips Collection Opens ‘Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea’

Milton Avery went to Gloucester, Massachusetts, to “live like an artist,” then brought Adolph Gottlieb and Mark Rothko along for summers of creative exchange. In Washington, D.C., The Phillips Collection’s “Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea” brings together watercolors and color-drenched canvases, tracing what those Cape Ann days set in motion.

Tate St Ives Spotlights Wilhelmina Barns-Graham

What does a landscape feel like in the body? Scottish artist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham spent eight decades exploring that question through art shaped by sensation and memory. The retrospective at Tate St Ives in Cornwall, England, is the most comprehensive survey of her work, moving from early landscapes and studio interiors to later works alive with bold color and sweeping gestures.

Taylor Swift, take note: famously hard-to-get-into New York City hotspot The Corner Store has officially landed at The Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas, marking its first-ever location outside Manhattan. Expect its adventurous martinis, signature wood-paneled interiors by Rockwell Group, and a handful of Vegas-exclusive menu additions, including a Butcher’s Counter serving up wagyu tomahawk and porterhouse steaks.

#6712. The Health Benefits of Stair Climbing

We’ve all heard the recommendation to “take the stairs” instead of the escalator or elevator. Not only is it an easy way to squeeze more movement into your day, but research has linked stair climbing to better cardiovascular health and longevity. Even the famously long-lived residents of Barbagia, Sardinia—one of the world’s so-called Blue Zones—spend much of their day navigating steep hills and staircases.

But nutritionist Marián García—better known as Boticaria García, author of Mujeres de Hierro (Iron Women)—takes the humble staircase one step further.

According to Garcia, the benefits of climbing stairs are more numerous than many of us realize: the activity can help increase energy expenditure, improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthen muscles and bones, and even blunt post-meal blood sugar spikes—benefits that become especially valuable after 40, when metabolism, muscle mass, and hormone levels begin to shift.

According to García, consistency matters more than intensity. “When I started running, I incorporated stairs on my way home as the finishing touch to my workout,” she writes in Mujeres de Hierro. “Over time, the habit grew, and today I not only seek out stairs wherever I go—whether at work or in hotels—but sometimes I even climb them carrying grocery bags or suitcases.”

You don’t even need to spend hours on the stair climber at the gym to reap the benefits. García’s recommendation is easy to remember: Simply aim to climb three flights of stairs three times a day. The advice comes from a study in which sedentary adults climbed approximately 60 steps—about three flights—at a brisk pace three times a day, three days a week, for six weeks. By the end of the study, participants had significantly improved their cardiovascular fitness.

García recommends aiming for an effort level of around six or seven out of 10. “You should be breathing harder and your legs should know they’re working,” she says. “You don't need to sprint or arrive at the top completely out of breath—but you shouldn’t be climbing while looking at your phone, either.”

Once stair climbing becomes part of your routine, García suggests making two small adjustments.

Take two steps at a time: “Your stride lengthens, and your glutes and legs have to work harder. That muscle contraction also increases the stimulus on the bone,” she explains.

Vary your pace: Alternate between climbing quickly and more slowly rather than maintaining the same rhythm throughout. “Changing the pace increases the demand and prevents your legs from climbing on autopilot,” she explains.

The strategy is based on what’s known as Frost’s mechanostat—the idea that bone adapts to the loads placed upon it. “If bone receives sufficient and varied stimuli, it understands that it needs to stay strong. If we never challenge it, it becomes complacent,” García says.

One of stair climbing’s most surprising benefits has to do with blood sugar. “Stairs are like a mini gym between floors,” García says. “They engage your glutes and legs, get your heart pumping, break up sedentary time, and increase energy expenditure.”

Research has also found that just one minute of stair climbing after a meal can help reduce the post-meal rise in blood glucose. “No, it doesn’t cancel out the pudding for dessert,” García jokes, “but it gets your muscles to remove some of the glucose circulating in your blood.”

Of course, she isn’t suggesting that stair climbing replaces strength training or cardio. Instead, she sees it as something even more valuable: a tiny habit that’s easy to repeat every day. “It’s a small, repeated action that gradually builds up your health savings,” she notes.
