#6645. In Puerto Rico, It's Not Thanksgiving—It's Sanguiving

Puerto Rican Thanksgiving is an exhilarating holiday remix. Think turkey marinated in garlic, lime, and oregano, then stuffed with fried green plantains and chicharrón mofongo. Gravy is more likely to be made with guava than with giblets, and flan stands in for apple pie. “Pumpkin spice” is nowhere to be found; here, the local winter squash calabaza takes center stage. And in lieu of warm apple cider, sweet coconut water is sipped beachside straight from a coco.

Thanksgiving is just as cherished in Puerto Rico as it is on the mainland. Celebrated locally since the early 20th century, shortly after the United States invaded in 1898, it marks the beginning of the island’s rambunctious holiday season. It is also a favorite of chef and restaurateur Giovanna Huyke, who over four decades has become the feast’s culinary authority in Puerto Rico.

I meet with Huyke, widely considered the Puerto Rican answer to Julia Child, on a hot summer day at SatoFino, a neon-hued, woman-owned restaurant in San Juan. The bartender quickly spies her—Huyke is a regular, and her signature red hair makes her easy to spot—and prepares the chef ’s go-to drink, a stiff Manhattan. We settle into our barstools, readying to plan what will ultimately unfurl into an epic cooking adventure. Huyke has a propensity for them, she tells me. In the preceding days she traveled to Atlanta to cook for Ser Familia—a nonprofit that specializes in supporting Hispanic families—before she rushed back to Caguas, a city 20 miles south of San Juan, where she fed VIPs attending the Miss Universe Puerto Rico pageant. Then she raced across the island to teach a traditional-methods cooking class in San Germán, the second-oldest city in Puerto Rico. Now, she’ll show me how to prepare a Puerto Rican Thanksgiving feast.

A vueltita through the Plaza del Mercado de Río Piedras with a fresh haul of groceries, in preparation for Sanguiving.

“We have a rich and resilient food history—it came from necessity, lack, and a bounty from the land,” Huyke says. It’s a complex cuisine informed by both a deep agricultural heritage and a modern reliance on imported and shelf-stable ingredients, which, despite many obstacles, manages to emerge beautiful and full of flavor—the continuation of a culinary evolution ongoing for centuries. “Our food comes from Spain, Indigenous Taíno people, and [enslaved] West Africans,” Huyke continues. “But it grew from our land and from our history, mixing every influence in our pilónes and our cauldrons.”

Being around Huyke is a joy. A local TV personality, newspaper columnist, and cookbook writer since the late ’80s, Huyke has taught generations of Puerto Rican home cooks how to prepare the island’s most treasured dishes. Among them was my grandmother, Sara, who I call Tata. Like many members of the Puerto Rican diaspora, my family traveled back to the island for the festivities, alternating each year between Thanksgiving and Christmas. We’d enter Hartsfield- Jackson International Airport in Atlanta in heavy winter coats and leave San Juan’s Luis Muños Marín in shorts and tank tops.

Tata’s Thanksgiving table centered on the expected turkey, but her stuffing was exceedingly Puerto Rican. To a base of Pepperidge Farm stuffing mix, she added picadillo: ground beef cooked with sofrito—the fragrant blend of garlic, onions, peppers, and the punchy native herb culantro that is the cornerstone of the Puerto Rican palate—and pimiento-stuffed Manzanilla olives, all seasoned with the golden spice blend sazón. When Tata died I inherited a weathered copy of Huyke’s 2004 recipe booklet Celebraciones. Within it were recipes that clearly informed Tata’s tremendous Thanksgiving menu; it turned out Huyke had been influencing my holiday for even longer than I knew.

Although formally known in Puerto Rico as El Día de Acción de Gracias, in true Boricua fashion, Thanksgiving is often referred to as Sanguiving, a play on words that gestures to the Roman Catholicism that remains the region’s predominant religion. It’s also El Día del Pavo, which directly translates to “Turkey Day,” and Sangiving, spelled like it sounds. We islanders have a fondness for clever, shortened expressions, an example of our natural tendency toward Puertorriqueñizar—in English, “to make Puerto Rican.”

A stall brims with large slabs of local calabaza.

“Our adobo goes on the turkey, and all the sides have something to do with sofrito,” Huyke tells me, walking me through the standard Puerto Rican Thanksgiving table. In Puerto Rico, adobo takes two forms—one wet and one dry. Each is a spectacular blend of Spanish, African, and Indigenous ingredients and techniques—garlic, onion, peppers, and herbs pounded in a wooden mortar and pestle with Taíno roots called a pilón, binding the island’s ancestral and colonial cultures.

Puerto Ricans officially became American citizens (and draft eligible) in 1917, just weeks before the US entered World War I. As many as 20,000 locals served, and Puerto Rican soldiers have played a role in every US military conflict since. In many respects, Thanksgiving traditions rooted en la isla are part of a broader military promise: American soldiers always eat well on Thanksgiving Day. Puerto Rican soldiers brought many wartime foodways home with them, and this combined with government subsidies means that today staples can at times feel military-adjacent—especially given the reliance on shelf-stable foods required by a storm-prone island. Over time, the territory’s once agrarian economy (centered around sugar, coffee, and tobacco exports) was transformed into an industrial manufacturing system. Puerto Ricans still consume many foods like tinned corned beef, Vienna sausages, Spam, club soda crackers, and canned vegetables; roughly 85 percent of all food in Puerto Rico is imported.

When Huyke’s father, Hector, served in the Korean War, he encountered the military’s famously bland instant mashed potatoes. From then on, he flat-out refused the dish except during holidays, when Huyke’s mother, Alice (herself a trained cooking instructor), made an impossible-to-resist version: yellow potatoes slowly simmered in cream, enriched with chicken bouillon, then whipped until fluffy with butter. Today a garlicky variation features on Huyke’s Sanguiving table.

Huyke, for her part, wants to steer Puerto Rican cuisine away from processed ingredients and back toward fresh foods—not only because they’re healthier, but also because they are richer in flavor and better convey the layered story of the island’s culinary heritage. She favors from-scratch dishes that lean on regional bounty, from Indigenous staples like maize, peppers, yuca, and other root vegetables to later introductions like plantains and coconuts.

Ají dulce (sweet peppers) are essential to local cuisines across Latin America and the Caribbean—and Chef Giovanna's Sanguiving table.

The best way to explain, she tells me, is to cook together. A few weeks later Huyke joins me in my own kitchen in North Carolina. I quickly learn that cooking alongside her is a lot like having your own personal instructor. At each step she explains how she’s arrived at a certain preparation and why she uses specific ingredients over others. It’s clearly a familiar role: Education remains a central focus for Huyke, and she counts among her mentees young women like Natalia Vallejo, the island’s first James Beard Award–winning chef. She frequently enlists up-and-coming chefs to cook alongside her and makes herself available for mentoring phone calls. I now feel lucky that I can count myself among them.

Although Huyke auditions new Sanguiving dishes every year, Puerto Rican favorites are always on the menu, many of them influenced by her mother’s recipes. Key among them is yuca stuffing—or “estuffing,” as Puerto Ricans commonly pronounce it. Huyke’s family version, Agüeybaná stuffing, is named for the island’s powerful Taíno chief who led the local people at the time of the Spanish invasion in 1493. Huyke peels and then grates fresh yuca before grinding it to a paste in the food processor. Meanwhile, she instructs me to sauté sofrito in olive oil before adding ground and salt pork, annatto, herbs, and aromatics. It’s all piled into a high-walled dish and baked.

Next we turn our attention to pastelón, a lasagna-like layered casserole of fried sweet plantains and creamy queso fresco. The dish was likely born in New York City, where Puerto Rican and Italian communities converged, before finding its way to the island.

“The Puerto Rican and Italian diasporas were physically close in New York during the ’50s—they were exposed to lasagna and mozzarella,” she explains.

Then come more sides. Gandules, or pigeon peas, are a treasured crop. Though they’re frequently served with rice at Sanguiving and other times of year—arroz con gandules is Puerto Rico’s national dish— Huyke instead opts for an escabèche-style salad that marries gandules with tomatoes, avocado, and herbs in a tangy vinaigrette. Another island staple, canned beets, gets a fresh reinterpretation as Huyke roasts a local-grown variety and tops them with crumbled queso fresco.

Huyke’s Sanguiving turkey rests on a banana leaf bed and is adorned with freshly picked wildflowers from the rainforest.

Many Puerto Rican families choose pernil, or roast pork shoulder, as their Sanguiving centerpiece. It is typically marinated overnight in an adobo of minced garlic, sour orange juice, olive oil, oregano, salt, and pepper. But Huyke sticks to turkey, brining it first in a mixture of salt, brown sugar, dried bay leaves, fresh herbs, and peppercorns before pushing butter under the skin and brushing the bird with a blend of rum, melted butter, and guava jelly. Huyke preserves the drippings for a tangy-sweet guava-infused gravy. She also shows me how to make ajilímojilí, a highly adaptable, herbaceous sauce of garlic, ají dulce peppers (similar to bell but fruitier and more delicate), culantro, cilantro, olive oil, vinegar, and her own signature addition: a copious amount of capers. Guests will drizzle it over nearly every dish on her Sanguiving table, she tells me.

After hours of cooking and using every imaginable tool, from a traditional pilón to a modern Vitamix blender, we sit down to enjoy the fruits of our frying, molding, steaming, sautéing, and roasting. The result is unmistakably an American Thanksgiving spread, refracted kaleidoscopically through a fresh, colorful Puerto Rican lens.

Puerto Ricans have both embraced and resisted US imperialism at various points. There always lingers the question of statehood, which exists alongside the island’s long-standing and active independence movement. As Huyke’s cooking demonstrates, this push-pull relationship only continues to play out in all sorts of dynamic ways.

“I believe every cuisine evolves,” she says. “But traditions should be kept and taught. So we do not lose the roots that make us unique.”

#6643. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6642. Popular Thanksgiving Product Recalled From Costco Shelves Over Concerning Contamination Risk

Here's what shoppers need to know ahead of the holiday.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Costco members, listen up. A popular Thanksgiving topping is being recalled over concerns about possible cleaning chemical contamination. Here's what to watch for.

Costco is recalling its Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream ahead of the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday. The recall covers 15-ounce cans sold between October 11 and October 31, 2026, including those purchased in three-packs.

To identify the affected product, check for item number 1777000, item code AC50, and a best-if-used-by date of April 2, 2027. The cans must also have a printed timestamp between 00:35 and 02:45.

The whipped cream was sold at Costco warehouses in 12 states: Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, and Wisconsin.

Producer Alamance Foods voluntarily recalled the product after learning that one batch may contain a small amount of a cleaning chemical. According to a November 7 letter sent to Costco members, some shoppers reported a chemical smell and taste.

The company said no serious adverse health effects requiring medical care had been reported. The notice does not identify the chemical or say how it may have gotten into the whipped cream.

If your can matches the affected lot and timestamp, stop using it and return it to your local Costco for a full refund. The company's notice also includes photographs of the can and its printed code to help shoppers identify the product.

For questions or concerns, contact Alamance Foods at customer.care@alamancefood.com.

#6641. This Olympic Volleyball Player’s Kona Village Wedding Was a Heartfelt Tribute to His Hawaiian Roots

As two UCLA volleyball players, Susannah Muno and Micah Ma’a often crossed paths. “The athlete community at UCLA was pretty tight-knit, so we ran into each other here and there. But we were never really in the same circles,” says Susannah, who goes by Zana. It wasn’t until a dare during their senior year that they truly connected. “I remember so vividly being on the bus with my team during a road trip when I got an Instagram DM from Micah. I screamed,” she says. “Naturally, I passed my phone around to the entire team, and then we all screamed.” It turns out that Micah and two teammates each chose someone for the others to DM. “Very college,” laughs Zana. “Three girls on our team got DMs from three guys on the men’s team that day. Two of those three couples are still together.”

Micah’s friends clearly put fate into motion. Zana and Micah made plans to see each other and that first night, they talked, laughed, and even cried until morning. “Somewhere in the middle of that night, I realized that how hot he was was actually the least interesting thing about him,” says Zana. “I won’t go so far as to say it was love at first sight. But I do think that from that first day together, we both knew there wasn’t really a version of our lives where we didn’t want the other person in it.”

Over the next six years, the two navigated a long-distance relationship as they competed professionally around the world. Micah even represented the United States at the 2024 Paris Olympics and helped the Indoor Volleyball team win a bronze medal. Two weeks later, on August 19th, 2024, Micah proposed. “We drove our little golf cart to dinner at a restaurant in our beach town that I had been wanting to try all summer,” recalls Zana. “After dinner, we went for a walk along the beach, as we often do, and that’s when it happened!” The couple celebrated at home together in their “own little bubble of happiness.” Family and friends helped them pull together an engagement party in just a few days to celebrate. “The very next day, Micah and I packed our bags and left for his next season abroad—a pretty fitting start to the next chapter of our lives,” she says.

The couple decided to tie the knot on May 24, 2026, in Kona Village on the Big Island of Hawai’i. “Micah is Native Hawaiian, and his Hawaiian culture is something deeply rooted within him and his family,” explains Zana. “Having the privilege of getting married on the island of Hawaiʻi, on land that feels so raw, untouched, and sacred, was something we didn’t take lightly. Throughout the entire planning process, we wanted to honor and respect the culture of this land and its people. We kept coming back to one simple vision for the wedding: a sense of place.”

Curating a thoughtful group of vendors made this dream come to life. Alison Rose Events managed planning, while the bride and her future sister-in-law helped lead the design process. “I spent so much time finding the right people—people who felt like family and, in many cases, actually were,” says Zana. “Each of our musicians was a friend of the family, which made every space feel that much more intimate. It wasn’t a stranger playing a violin; it was a friend sharing his gift with us on one of the most meaningful days of our lives.”

Florals, in particular, were a key part of their wedding weekend’s vision. Ren McDonald of Renko Floral foraged greenery and blooms from all over the island—including some family members’ backyards—to create organic arrangements that felt true to the environment. Lei worn throughout the weekend were also hand-made by Micah’s family. “None of these details were about creating something simply for the sake of beauty,” says Zana. “They were about making the weekend feel like us and, just as importantly, making it feel like Hawaiʻi.”

With a full weekend of celebration planned throughout Kona Village, the couple needed to fill their wardrobes with the perfect pieces for each event. Zana looked back in her closet for her first bridal look. “Micah and I actually got legally married the year before at Kona Village with just the two of us and our officiant,” says the bride. “I wore a Hanne Bloch two-piece silk tulle set, and we stood barefoot on the lanai of our hale as we said our vows. When it came time to choose what I would wear to our welcome party exactly one year later, it felt only right to wear that same outfit again.” The groom also donned a piece from the past for the party, choosing to wear his Tūtū’s (grandfather’s) aloha shirt as a nostalgic touch.

The next day was full of activities, starting with a pickleball tournament with a Wimbledon white dress code. The bride wore a matching Alo set and popped on a custom hat the couple had made for all their guests. “Of course, Micah won,” says Zana. “I’m still not sure his partner touched a single ball, but that’s beside the point.” The couple then spent the afternoon poolside with all their guests. Zana kept it carefree in a Monday Swimwear bikini with a Solaqua cover-up. “We had fresh coconuts filled with a little rum float, lounged around the pool, and eventually ended up taking one huge group swim out to the lily pad in the ocean,” she says.

The bride’s next ensemble made a bigger statement. “For our rehearsal dinner, I wore a shell-and-fringe dress by British designer Kilentar that weighed 22 pounds,” Zana says. “The dress was everything that night was: fun, organic, flirty, and a little unexpected. It floated and moved so beautifully, and with literally every step I took, the shells made the most incredible sound.” Micah complemented her natural-toned look in a custom linen button-down and trousers.

Zana at first struggled to find a dress for the wedding day until Danielle Frankel opened her bridal boutique in Los Angeles. “I tried on my dress just days after it had come down the runway, and immediately, my mind was made up,” she says of her strapless gown. “The organic, lightweight linen fabric mirrored the textures of the landscape around us, while the bubble hem gave the dress this beautiful shape and movement that reminded me of the ocean and the lava rock.” Micah had one request for Zana’s bridal ensemble: he asked her to wear a veil. A style from Danielle Frankel was the perfect fit. “I loved it so much that I vowed to myself she will be worn again,” she says.

For Micah’s walk down the aisle, he had a bespoke suit made at The Imperial Tailoring Company in Moscow. “He had been away for the eight months leading up to the wedding, so having a suit made together in the U.S. simply wasn’t possible,” explains Zana. “Instead, we set out to find the best tailor we could in Russia and ended up creating the most incredible custom suit for him.” She adds, “In a funny way, even his wedding look became a reflection of the life we were living at the time.”

During the reception, Zana had two outfit changes. First, she wore a mini dress that was crafted from the skirt of her mother’s wedding dress. “Wearing a piece of my mother’s dress was so much more emotional than I anticipated,” she reflects. Her final look was an Elce linen two-piece set with a backless halter top and pants. “It was very me—comfortable, freeing, and effortless,” Zana says.

Zana’s jewelry throughout the weekend was actually all pieces borrowed from her mother’s best friend, Lisa Wehrly, whom the bride sees as a mentor and role model. “I was able to wear pieces from her collection throughout the celebrations, each one carrying its own stories and history,” she says.

The celebrations kicked off on Friday night with a casual welcome event overlooking the ocean. Cocktails, bites, and conversation led to an unexpected turn. “In classic Hawaiian get-together fashion, it wasn’t long before someone picked up a microphone,” says Zana. “Micah’s sister, Mehana Maʻa, took the mic for a few songs, followed by Micah himself, who sang ‘I’m Yours’ by Jason Mraz. He then somehow transitioned into a hilarious, completely off-the-cuff freestyle, welcoming everyone to this beautiful place and telling them to get ready for the best weekend. Everyone absolutely erupted. It was spontaneous and so perfectly Micah, and it immediately set the tone for the weekend.”

The next day was filled with pickleball, poolside drinks, and connection under the Hawaiian sun. Then, the night turned more intimate with a rehearsal dinner in a Kiawe grove with an open-air barbecue. The couple, who love to host, wanted the evening to feel like a night at their home with speeches added in. “Of course, Micah and I decided it was necessary to make our way around dinner, taking a shot with every single table,” says Zana. “Needless to say, the energy escalated pretty quickly. Everyone loosened up, we ate incredible food, laughed all night, and had the absolute best time.”

However, the night didn’t end just yet. The couple and friends piled into golf carts back to their villa. “The second I walked through the door, my 22-pound dress hit the floor, and everyone jumped straight into the pool in their clothes. I opted for slightly less clothing and did a little skinny-dipping,” says Zana. “My mom and dad came out of bed and jumped in wearing their pajamas, while my brother and the rest of our family were mildly appalled that I was completely naked. It was chaotic and ridiculous and absolutely perfect.” She adds, “It will forever be one of my favorite memories from the weekend.”

The ceremony took place the next day on the black sand beach surrounded by lava rock and cliffs overlooking the ocean. “It was dramatic. It was raw. It was perfect,” describes Zana. The bride walked down the aisle with her father to “Somewhere Over the Rainbow,” and Micah’s best friend Evan Enriques officiated the proceedings. “The vows were, without question, the heart of it all,” remembers the bride. “There was nothing gentle or lighthearted about them. They were genuine and from the heart—raw and unfiltered, just like the place where we stood. From what we’ve heard since the wedding, there wasn’t a dry eye in sight.” The couple both felt as if everything else fell away and they were speaking to each other from the heart. “It was one of the best moments of my life,” says the bride.

The reception kicked off with cocktail hour, followed by dinner and dancing. “Micah’s seven-year-old niece opened dinner with a prayer in ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi, which was such a special way to begin the evening,” says Zana. Speeches were followed by a hula performance by Micah’s three sisters and niece, then a fire knife dance from the groom’s best friend, Larry “Tui” Tuileta. “Before long, Micah and Evan had joined him,” says Zana. Watching the three of them together was so special because this wasn’t something created for the wedding—they have been doing versions of this at family parties since they were little.”

“The rest of the night is honestly a blur in the best possible way,” says the bride. Dancing was followed by another late-night jump into the pool at the villa after-party. “Eventually, it was just Micah and me and a handful of our closest friends sitting around the dinner table, talking until four in the morning. A couple of them stayed so late that they left the table and headed almost directly to the airport for their flights home.”

“It felt like the perfect way to end the weekend,” adds the bride. “We’re just heartbroken that we can’t do it all over again!”

Exactly one year before our welcome party, Micah and I were legally married at Kona Village, just the two of us. It felt only right to rewear the stunning Hanne Bloch silk tulle two-piece set I wore that day. I'm so glad I did. It was such a special way to bring a piece of that intimate day into our wedding weekend. —Zana

It’s happening! I remember walking up to the Moana Lawn and thinking, “Oh my gosh, it’s really here.” Seeing everything I had envisioned come to life brought this incredible combination of relief and excitement. Suddenly, it was all real. —Zana

I wanted our welcome flowers to be inspired by the plumeria flower lei so often given upon arriving in Hawaiʻi. To make this vision come to life, our florist, Ren MacDonald-Balasia, went down to Kealakekua and met with a very special retired gardener who let her cut and purchase blooms directly from her yard. She had the longest oncidium orchids growing out of the lava rock wall that were about 36 inches a stem. She used them like vines and wove them through the butter yellow shower-tree blooms to create an unexpected arrangement of yellow en masse—intentionally combined together to invoke curiosity, like it could be one flower, not two. —Zana

My grandma and one of my best friends, hand-in-hand and cocktail in hand. Exactly the spirit we were hoping for all weekend! —Zana

This photo captures the pure joy I felt watching all of my favorite people arrive for our wedding weekend. Savannah is my childhood best friend, and I had the privilege of standing beside her during her own magical wedding celebrations. Now it was my turn. There is something so special about moving through life’s biggest chapters alongside the people who have known you the longest. —Zana

In nearly every childhood photo I have with my mom, I’m holding on tight. She’s always meant the world to me. Living overseas means I don’t get to hug her nearly as often as I’d like, so when I do, I never take it for granted. —Micah

Are you kidding?! The sunset, the people, the weather, the place, and THAT MAN! No words will ever do it justice. —Zana

In this moment, I remember feeling exactly the way I used to in college while watching Micah play volleyball at UCLA. His charisma and energy are unlike anything I’ve ever experienced, and I think everyone there was completely charmed by him in that moment. It was just so perfectly Micah. —Zana

This photo captures my wife perfectly. Her joy, her spirit, and her enthusiasm for life. —Micah

My niece has been asking her mom nonstop if she can please go back to Uncle Micah and Aunty Zana’s wedding. I’m not sure anyone had a better time than she did. —Micah

Everyone hard at work putting together their scouting reports.

Obviously, Micah won pickleball. And no, nobody took it easy on him. —Zana

For our save-the-dates, I embroidered our wedding details onto the same linen my dress was made from. They simply read, “Micah and Susannah – Kona Village, HI – May 24, 2026.” My Grandma Sue, never one to miss an opportunity, used hers to customize her hat for the pickleball tournament. —Zana

I’m pretty sure I didn’t stop smiling the entire weekend! —Zana

We’re a competitive bunch, so naturally, we had to hire legitimate referees for our pickleball tournament. —Micah

The long farm tables, the warmth of the fire, and the soft lighting made the evening feel less like a formal rehearsal dinner and more like a family dinner in our own home.

We wanted the florals to feel like a celebration of Hawaiʻi. Our florist Ren sourced rare bromeliad blooms that were punctuated by ripe and shiny mountain apples that were sourced from the Hilo farmer’s market. She wanted the arrangements to invoke a sense of lava flowing through the rocks, so in addition to the fiery color palette, she used hala lei made from the pandanus fruit to slope down the actual lava rocks at the base of the piece.

Hand in hand, on our way to the rehearsal dinner. —Micah

My beautiful mother made a special lei from naupaka, the flower we had chosen as the symbol of our wedding. —Micah

My two younger sisters gave such an amazing speech, starting the night off in a way that made it feel like one big family dinner. People reminisced about old times and our stories became even grander than the last time we had told them. —Micah

My relationship with my sisters has never been a rollercoaster full of highs and lows. Instead, for as long as I can remember, it has been a steady source of the most loyal and loving support that I have experienced. —Micah

I feel like one of the luckiest people in the world to have parents who have supported every dream I’ve ever had. My wedding was no exception. Watching my dad beam as he saw me living out my fairytale wedding meant everything to me. —Zana

I might be biased, but this was one of the best meals of my life! The warmth of the fire, the local vegetables, and a family-style dinner beneath the lights and trees. I’ll never get over it. —Zana

Our niece and goddaughter loved my Kilentar shell-and-fringe dress just as much as I did! I remember seeing it for the first time and thinking, “This isn’t a want. It’s a need!” —Zana

A wedding-morning canoe ride—just the two of us!

The ocean has always been such an important place for us. It’s a place of healing and a place of cleansing. Before we make a big move across the world or a big decision in life, we have always made sure to jump in the water. —Micah

She sells seashells by the seashore. And he buys them just to spend a little more time with her. —Micah

Growing up, The Parent Trap was my all-time favorite movie. There’s a scene at camp where they’re raising and lowering the flag that has always stuck with me. When we started dreaming up our wedding weekend, I wanted it to have that same nostalgic feeling of summer camp. And, of course, no summer camp would be complete without a flag. —Zana

Seeing my wedding dress hanging beside the mini dress made from my mother’s wedding gown was incredibly meaningful. My parents’ marriage is something I’ve always admired and aspired to, and having such a special piece of their wedding day woven into my own felt like a beautiful full-circle moment. —Zana

The most incredible human I’ve ever known. My mom. —Zana

From the moment Micah and I met, we shared the same greatest priority in life: our families. So when it came time to decide who I wanted around me while getting ready, the answer felt obvious. I wanted to be surrounded by the women who have shaped my life. They wore the most beautiful House of Pacific dresses, while I got ready in a Danielle Frankel robe. —Zana

The dramatic contrast of my billowing white Danielle Frankel gown against the jagged black lava still takes my breath away. —Zana

The two men who have lifted me up and carried me through every chapter of my life. —Zana

Moments before walking down the aisle. I was more nervous than I’d expected. I think the magnitude of what was about to happen finally caught up with me. —Zana

One of the greatest gifts God has ever given me is this man. My father. —Micah

I found this suit in an underground shop near Red Square in Moscow. The story is far too long to tell, as so many of our stories from living overseas tend to be. But getting married in Hawaiʻi wearing a suit I found in Russia just about sums up our lives. —Micah

Micah and I had originally chosen another ceremony location on the property, but the moment we saw this spot, we knew our plans had to change. The drama of the black lava against the crashing blue waves felt like the perfect setting for this chapter of our story. —Zana

We wanted the ceremony florals to feel as though they were growing naturally from the landscape, complementing the beauty of the island rather than competing with it. Our florist so beautifully juxtaposed the sharpness of local foraged Kona grasses with the softness of cream colored oncidium orchids. The grasses created waves while the orchids created fluttering foamy moments, indicative of the ocean behind the ceremony.

Our guests making their way to the ceremony.

I have dreamt of this moment hundreds of times since I was a little girl. I always imagined my dad would cry because, if you know him, you know he’s a big softie. But somehow, neither of us did. Instead, we laughed and smiled in complete disbelief at just how perfect everything felt. —Zana

I’ve never experienced a moment where I was so completely unaware of everything else happening in the world. Watching your future wife walk down the aisle is a feeling that can’t really be explained. It’s something you can only understand once you’ve experienced it. —Micah

Micah’s hands have always been one of my favorite things about him. Seeing a wedding ring on his finger felt completely surreal. —Zana

For the reception, Ren carried the natural beauty of the island through to our dinner tables. The tables were full of symbolism and native material. One of the most special symbols were the Naupaka branches and flowers, an ode to the Hawaiian legend of Naupaka and the symbol we chose to represent their wedding. There was also local gardenia from Oahu on every table, a very special flower to Micah’s family. The gardenia were hand carried on the plane, and the extra effort to bring them over was worth it as their fragrance wafted through the reception tables with each passing Kona breeze. —Zana

#6637. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6636. 3 Easy Hacks To Make Instant Mashed Potatoes WAY Better

You might prefer homemade mashed potatoes, but sometimes you just need a shortcut—and on days like that, grabbing the box is WAY easier. But while the back-of-the-box directions will yield just-fine results, a few easy hacks will give you much better results.

As a recipe developer and professional cook, I don’t often make instant mashed potatoes, but I was excited by the challenge of leveling them up—without adding a bunch of extra ingredients or steps that take the convenience out of this convenience food. So I tried making instant mashed potatoes every way I could think of (including the way the box says!). In the end, I found three tricks that, while super simple, massively improve that final bowl of mashed potatoes.

Here are three ways to instantly upgrade instant mashed potatoes.

Most boxes tell you to rehydrate instant mashed potato flakes in hot water enriched with a little butter and a few tablespoons of milk—but I’m going all in on the milk here. The extra dairy really fills out the flavor of the mashed potato and makes it creamier—especially if you’re using a higher-fat milk, like whole or 2%.

When swapping milk for water, it’s best to increase the liquid amount just slightly. For some reason (totally scientific, I’m sure!), the potato flakes require more milk than water to hydrate properly. I recommend 2 extra tablespoons for every half cup of instant mashed potatoes.

Also, add the extra milk the box typically calls for. If you leave it out, the potatoes will be dry. When I was testing, I found it didn’t really matter when that second amount of milk went into the pan (at the beginning versus just before the potatoes), but some boxes emphasize putting it in cold just before adding the potatoes—so if you want to do that to make you feel safer, be my guest!

All the instant mashed potatoes I made lacked seasoning—until I doubled the salt. Then they were perfect. Now here’s the thing: I was testing with Diamond Crystal kosher salt, which is less salty by volume than table salt or Morton’s kosher. The back of the instant mashed potato box didn’t specify what type of salt they used, so if they tested with a fine salt or Morton’s kosher, maybe ¼ teaspoon was the perfect amount. But in my kitchen with Diamond Crystal, it was woefully underseasoned.

Maybe you’re nervous about oversalting and don’t want to double or even slightly increase the salt right away. But regardless, I’m begging you: Taste those potatoes before you serve them and don’t feel bad if you have to add another hefty pinch.

You might assume that mashed potatoes should be made in a pot—I definitely did. But the fluffiest, creamiest instant potatoes I made in this whole testing process came from a wide, high-sided sauté pan. The reason for this? Absolute science.

When adding the instant potato flakes to the hot liquid, the goal is to distribute them as evenly as possible without working them too much. Yes, the back of the box says to “stir” the potatoes in, but in testing, I quickly discovered that even a few strokes can quickly lead to gummy potatoes.

Here’s where the pan size comes in. Using a wide pan increases the liquid's surface area, so you can sprinkle the potatoes evenly over the top and pat them down into the liquid instead of stirring. From there, let them stand until they’ve absorbed the liquid, then give them a few stirs. Trust me: They’ll be way fluffier because you messed with them less!

(So long, easy-breezy summer days—we miss you already.) You can wear the cutest outfit known to mankind, and your clunky, rubber-soled winter boots will instantly ruin the vibe. Why must most winter boots be so hideous? Why are they always so big and bulky? So overpowering? Surely, I can trek through the snow without having to wear the shoe equivalent of a monster truck!

Historically, this style conundrum has led me to forgo winter boots altogether: You can often find me stubbornly walking through a blizzard in my trusty sneakers or loafers—my socks instantly soaked, my toes frozen. But with a serious snowstorm impending, the annual quest to find actually-cute winter boots has begun, and taken on more urgency than ever. I simply can’t go on like this. And who better to ask for advice than some of my fellow Vogue colleagues?

#6633. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6631. Hot Honey Brussels Sprouts

These honey-glazed brussels sprouts are saucy, tangy-sweet, and have a bit of kick. Caramelizing the honey gives it a deeper, toastier sweetness. Vinegar, red pepper flakes, and a good dose of butter transform it into a sticky sauce that seeps into the nooks of each and every sprout. The recipe makes a generous amount: Use it all, or save some for drizzling on pizza a few days later.

The trick to perfectly charred brussels sprouts? Preheat the sheet pan, then arrange the halved sprouts cut side down on the hot metal. It might feel a little fussy flipping each sprout onto its flat side, but the deeply browned results are worth it.

Make the glaze while the sprouts roast or up to five days ahead, then toss everything together just before serving to preserve those crispy edges.

Glossy and pourable, about the consistency of warm maple syrup—not thick like caramel. The honey will foam as it cooks, and the mixture will bubble aggressively when you add the vinegar. Both are normal. The glaze will thicken a bit as it cools, so don’t worry if it seems slightly thin while still bubbling.

They have a noticeable kick, but they’re more tangy-sweet than fiery. The honey and butter temper the chile flakes. If you’re sensitive to spice, use less than the suggested ¾ tsp. or leave the flakes out entirely.

Place a rimmed baking sheet on bottom rack of oven; preheat to 450°. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, and ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil in a large bowl; sprinkle with ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and season with freshly ground black pepper.

Carefully remove baking sheet from oven. Using tongs, arrange brussels sprouts cut-side down on hot baking sheet. Roast brussels on bottom rack until softened and deeply browned, 15–25 minutes.

Meanwhile, bring ¼ cup honey to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat. Reduce heat to medium-low and cook, stirring often, until honey is a deep amber color but not burnt (it will be foamy, that’s okay), 3–4 minutes.

Remove from heat and add ⅓ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar (it will bubble up quite aggressively) and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes; whisk until sauce is smooth. Return saucepan to medium heat and add 3 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, whisking constantly, until glaze is glossy, bubbling, and slightly thickened, 3–4 minutes.

Transfer roasted brussels sprouts to a large bowl. Add half the hot honey glaze and scallions and toss to combine. Taste and add more glaze if desired. Transfer to a platter and top with lemon zest. Serve remaining glaze alongside.

Do ahead: Glaze can be made 5 days ahead; refrigerate after cooling.

#6630. Cranberry Pie

What People Are Saying:“I made 3 desserts this Thanksgiving and this was an absolute hit!! Everyone at the table raved about it including my super picky 7 year old who had herself seconds. Definitely a winner and will be making again.” - PurplePuzzle

Preheat your oven to 350° and grease a 9-inch pie plate with butter.

For the crust, grab a large bowl and mix together the Biscoff crumbs, melted butter, and a pinch of salt. Gently press this mixture into the bottom and up the sides of your greased pie plate.

Bake the crust until it turns golden and feels firm to the touch. Once done, set it aside on a wire rack to cool.

In a small bowl, mix the gelatin with some cold water and let it sit so it can bloom.

Next, for the filling, grab a medium saucepan, toss in the cranberries, brown sugar, orange juice, and zest, and bring it to a simmer over medium heat. Stir occasionally while the cranberries burst and the liquid has thickened slightly, which should take about 7 minutes.

Pour in the coconut milk, ginger, heavy cream, almond extract, and a little salt. Stir everything together and heat until it’s nice and steamy, but not quite simmering. Remove from the heat and stir in the bloomed gelatin until fully dissolved.

Now, blend the cranberry mixture until it’s super smooth—use whatever blender or food processor you have handy. Strain it into a bowl, toss out any solids, and let the mixture cool down to room temperature. Pour the cranberry filling into your crust and refrigerate until set, which should take at least 6 hours.

Serve with homemade whipped cream and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

This pie will keep for up to a week in the fridge and frozen for up to 5 months. Simply thaw it out in the fridge the next day and serve.

#6629. 40+ Affordable Jewelry Brands to Know and Shop in 2026

All products featured on Vogue are independently selected by our editors. However, we may earn affiliate revenue on this article and commission when you buy something.

To many, high quality, affordable jewelry may seem like an oxymoron. Among high-end fine jewelry offerings and high-street designer dupes, the middle ground may be hard to spot. Luckily, we’ve done the legwork. Today, there are plenty of jewelry brands offering quality pieces that won’t break the bank. Whether you’re searching for essentials, like stackable rings, everyday hoop earrings, and chain necklaces, that graciously won’t turn your skin green, or costume-level styles with a bit more character, you don’t need to spend a fortune to find your perfect piece.

Quality, of course, is key. The innovative materials and techniques of today’s modern brands create affordable jewelry that is durable and, with proper care, can last for years. Having purchased our share of styles that failed to last the season, over the years we’ve learned a few tricks of the trade. Gold vermeil, for example, is a less expensive, but still great-looking, alternative to solid gold. And for those on the hunt for a bit of sparkle, plenty of brands are making stunning designs with cubic zirconia. If your budget is a bit higher, lab-grown diamonds offer a more affordable alternative to mined stones. Explore our edit of the best affordable jewelry brands below.

Lié Studio creates elegant pieces that are timeless yet modern. Add these to your everyday essentials to elevate your capsule wardrobe, or pair with an elegant evening look.

Mejuri is a crowdpleaser that’s seemingly worn by everyone. It’s no surprise, though, as it offers great affordable alternatives to everyday fine jewelry.

Completedworks has long been a favorite here at Vogue. Its pieces offer a unique twist on the classics and many live within a $300 price limit.

Jenny Bird is one of our go-to’s for beautiful, chunky metals and sleek shapes. From huggie earrings to sleek bangles, these pieces are perfect for any occasion.

Founded in Copenhagen in 1982, Pandora charged into the global jewelry market in the early 2000s with its iconic customizable charm bracelets. Today, its vast collections extend well beyond those origins, encompassing everything from everyday staples to contemporary statement jewelry.

We love Laura Lombardi for great quality chains in the coolest styles and at affordable price points. Check out her earrings and rings as well for jewelry box essentials.

#6626. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6625. The Best Veterans Day Food Freebies, From Dunkin’ Donuts To Shake Shack Burgers

A guide to the restaurants thanking veterans with free meals and treats.

Every November 11, Americans celebrate and thank those who have served in our military. Veterans Day marks the anniversary of the 1918 armistice that ended World War I, but it wasn’t until 1954, after both World War II and the Korean War, that it changed nationally from Armistice Day to Veterans Day.

Active and retired military members can receive a free Original French Toast during operating hours for dine-in orders.

All active and retired military can enjoy a free donut.

Gold Star Families, active military, veterans, and first responders can get a complimentary 5-Course Teppanyaki Entree, including a choice of Hibachi Steak, Chicken, or Salmon. The offer is available for dine-in only and requires the purchase of an appetizer or starter.

Veterans and military members can order a free Spaghetti with Marinara or Meat Sauce with proof of veteran or military status by using the code VET26.

All current and retired military members can enjoy a complimentary buffet and beverage at Golden Corral locations nationwide.

Active-duty military and veterans can enjoy a complimentary choice of 10 Bone-In or Boneless Wings, Beer-Battered Fish & Chips, Steakburger, Chicken Caesar Salad, Buttermilk Crispy Chicken Sandwich, or Chicken BLT Tacos.

Veterans and active military personnel can enjoy a free small hot or iced coffee and a free donut of their choice.

Service members and veterans can receive a complimentary entrée and beverage from a special prix fixe menu, plus a Buy One Get One card, good for a pizza, pasta, or salad with the purchase of one on a return visit between November 12 and 25.

#6624. Sausage Stuffing Recipe

This sausage stuffing has everything you want on your Thanksgiving plate: crisp, craggy edges, a plush, savory center, and plenty of browned sausage throughout. Torn pieces of country-style bread soak up the broth and eggs without falling apart, turning golden and crunchy on top while staying tender underneath.

Breakfast sausage does much of the heavy lifting. Once browned, its drippings join plenty of butter to cook the onions, celery, and garlic. Fresh sage, parsley, and thyme bring balance, while optional fennel seeds add a little extra aromatic punch.

Uncooked pork breakfast sausage is the first choice. Typically seasoned with sage and black pepper, it brings familiar Thanksgiving flavors and plenty of richness. For some heat, choose spicy breakfast sausage. If you can't find the packaged kind or want to avoid pork, try making your own with our breakfast sausage recipe, using ground dark-meat turkey in place of pork.

This stuffing relies on the fat from breakfast sausage for its flavor. Want a vegetarian version? Our Simple-Is-Best Stuffing is a long-standing reader favorite and was the inspiration for this version; use that recipe with vegetable broth for a meat-free stuffing.

What’s the best bread for sausage stuffing?

Look for a sturdy country-style white loaf or sourdough with a relatively thin crust. Avoid soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy, and very crusty artisan loaves, which won’t absorb the broth as readily. Even if your bread is a day or two old, don’t skip drying it in the oven—that’s what helps the stuffing hold its shape.

Can I make sausage stuffing ahead of time?

You can dry the bread a day ahead and store it loosely covered at room temperature. For more ways to get ahead of Thanksgiving, including cooking, refrigerating, and reheating stuffing, see our make-ahead stuffing guide.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Grease a 13x9" baking dish with unsalted butter. Arrange one 1–1¼-lb. loaf country-style white bread, torn into 1" pieces, in a single layer on a large rimmed baking sheet and bake until dried out and golden around the edges, 30–40 minutes. Let cool.

Meanwhile, melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Cook 1 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, stirring and breaking into small pieces, until well browned and cooked through, 8–10 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind.

Reduce dial to medium heat and add remaining 8 Tbsp. unsalted butter to fat in pot; heat until melted. Cook 2 medium onions, finely chopped, 6 celery stalks, finely chopped, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. fennel seeds (if using), stirring occasionally, until onions are softened and golden around the edges, 12–15 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 2 cups low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth along with sausage, ½ cup (packed) coarsely chopped parsley, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped sage, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped thyme, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Whisk 3 large eggs and remaining 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth in a small bowl to combine, then stir into pot (don’t worry, eggs won’t scramble). Add bread to pot and toss gently to combine. Let sit, tossing occasionally, until liquid is almost completely absorbed, about 10 minutes.

Transfer stuffing to prepared dish (don’t pack or press down) and cover loosely with foil. Place dish on a clean large rimmed baking sheet and bake until stuffing is hot throughout (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 160°), 35–45 minutes. Increase oven temperature to 400° and remove foil (no need to remove stuffing from oven while heat increases). Continue to bake until stuffing is light golden brown on top, 25–30 minutes longer.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 1 day ahead; store loosely covered at room temperature. Stuffing can be assembled 1 day ahead; cover and chill. Bring to room temperature before baking.

#6623. Buttermilk Drop Biscuits

Recipe by Grace Vallo, Windham, New Hampshire

These buttermilk drop biscuits are tender, fluffy and buttery—no rolling, kneading or shaping required.

Buttermilk biscuits are, in my humble opinion, the perfect breakfast. They’re endlessly versatile—perfect for drowning in spicy sausage gravy, loading up with bacon and egg for a sandwich, or simply slathering with butter and jam. There’s really nothing a flaky biscuit can’t do. But I don’t always have the time or energy to roll and cut dough in the morning, and that’s where drop biscuits come in to save the day—or at least to stop me from opening up a can of refrigerated dough.

Making drop biscuits is almost improbably easy. You just stir together a few pantry staples to make the dough, plop spoonfuls on the pan and bake them until they’re perfectly golden brown. Whether you’re an experienced biscuit maker or looking to whip up your first-ever batch, this simple recipe delivers maximum payoff with just a couple of simple ingredients and a little bit of effort.

Preheat the oven to 425°F. As the oven warms up, combine the flour, baking soda, baking powder and salt in a large mixing bowl.

Editor’s Tip: Use a fork or a whisk to give the ingredients a good stir to make sure they’re all evenly incorporated.

Using a pastry cutter or a fork, cut the chilled butter into the dry ingredients until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs.

Editor’s Tip: You could use your hands to incorporate the butter into the flour, but use a light touch. The heat from your hands can melt the butter, and you don’t want that!

Stir the buttermilk into the crumb mixture just until it’s moistened.

Editor’s Tip: Grab your buttermilk straight from the refrigerator so it’s nice and cold. Mix just until you’ve formed a shaggy dough. It’s OK if your dough looks a little bit lumpy—you don’t want to over-mix it!

Drop the dough by 1/4-cupfuls 2 inches apart onto a greased baking sheet. Bake the biscuits until they’re golden brown on top, 11 to 13 minutes. Serve warm with butter, if desired.

Editor’s Tip: Don’t worry about making them perfectly round. A little bit of irregularity is part of the fun of drop biscuits.

Drop biscuits tend to be best right out of the oven, but you can place any leftovers inside an airtight storage container, where they’ll last on the counter for three to five days. Heat the biscuits up in a 200° oven for 5 to 10 minutes to bring them back to life.

There are several buttermilk substitutes, and the easiest one—white vinegar—is probably already in your pantry. Add 1 tablespoon of white vinegar to a 1-cup measure, then fill it the rest of the way with cold milk.

Make it a 3-ingredient recipe by swapping self-rising flour for the all-purpose flour. You won’t need the baking powder or the baking soda, as they’re already included in the flour mix. Mix the flour with the butter and buttermilk as directed to create an even easier batch of drop biscuits.

If your buttermilk drop biscuits are dense, check your baking powder. It’s possible that it’s expired, which could mean that it was too weak to help your dough rise. You may have also overworked the dough, which can result in a dense, tough biscuit.

#6622. Zimmermann Brought the Aussie Party Spirit Back to New York

A Zimmermann night out out was long overdue in New York City. It’s been some six years since sisters Nicky and Simone put on a party for their label around these parts—and you could hear Kylie Minogue’s voice blasting from the speakers the moment you pulled up to Indochine on Lafayette Street.

“The Irish and the Australians, it’s a lethal mix,” said Eve Hewson with a mischievous laugh. The Disclosure Day actress, who has recently relocated to Los Angeles, was more than happy to accept the invite to fly into town for the night—particularly after attending her first Zimmermann runway outing during Paris Fashion Week last month (her seat mate from the show, Charlotte Lawrence, quickly ran up and grabbed her with glee upon arrival).

Speaking of showing up to support sisters, Hewson divulged that there could indeed be a season 3 of the cult-favorite Apple TV show Bad Sisters “if people kick up enough of a fuss” to bring it back for another round of murderous fun. In the meantime, after a year where she’s been booked and busy, she’s ready to “just sleep” once the holiday season rolls around.

Around the buzzing restaurant, well-dressed groups broke off into huddles. Naomi Watts and Tommy Dorfman linked hands as they tattled, loved-up models Vivienne Rohner and Henry Rank canoodled in a corner, and sisters Jemima and Quentin Jones showed off their synchronized sultry black frocks at the step-and-repeat. Watts’s photographer brother, Ben, reunited with his fellow Aussies, and their accents audibly cranked up a notch as they cracked jokes together. DJ Amrit Tietz, also flying the flag for Australia, had rushed back from her cool mom platform Spread the Jelly’s most recent “Jellymoon” brand trip upstate to man the decks. (Hence the Kylie.)

Uma Thurman, who’s gracing screens in the just-dropped season 2 of Dexter: Resurrection, arrived in an all-black ensemble from the Cruise 2027 collection. After a quip was made about the extreme height difference between the 5’11” actress and Nicky Zimmermann, Thurman discreetly slipped her high heels off—prompting peals of laughter from the designer. “I hate heels anyway—I only ever wear them for work,” Thurman said, smiling.

As guests found their seats at a long table dressed in dramatic bundles of burgundy anthuriums, magenta dahlias, and amaranthus, a lace-clad Lawrence surprised the room with a performance of her new music, as well as Fleetwood Mac’s “Dreams.” Once the chocolate truffles and mini fruit tartlets were served, everyone was well and truly warmed up for the dance floor as Tietz returned to the DJ booth. Safe to say, more than a few pairs of shoes were kicked off.

#6621. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6618. The Minimalist ’90s-Style Coat Will Be Everywhere This Winter

The return of ’90s fashion is hardly new territory for the Vogue Shopping desk. But if 2026 has proved anything, it’s that our collective obsession with the decade isn’t going anywhere anytime soon. This year, Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy fever swept the headlines for months, coinciding with the release of Ryan Murphy’s hit drama Love Story, which (albeit after a few costume department consultations) sparked a return to the late fashion icon’s off-duty photographs, in search of styling inspiration.

“The online deluge of CBK content isn’t just generating likes; it’s been driving sales, too—a quick browse of the websites of Massimo Dutti or Reformation will give you some idea of just how swiftly brands have moved to capitalize on consumer fascination with this uncomplicated, clean aesthetic,” wrote Vogue’s Emma Spedding in her recent story on minimalism’s continued grip on our autumn wardrobes. She outlined the single-breasted longline coat as a key piece in achieving the sought-after CBK look–alongside a pencil skirt, turtleneck vest and simple leather bag.

Such coats were a cornerstone of the ’90s collections of Calvin Klein, Jil Sander, and Helmut Lang, characterised by (but not bound to) clean lines, understated single-breasted buttoning, discreet masculine lapels and a long, lean silhouette. Usually rendered in a palette of black, charcoal grey, beige, camel, and chocolate brown.

CBK was frequently photographed on the streets of New York in versions crafted from both wool and lighter-weight gabardine, styled off-duty with straight-leg jeans, oval sunglasses and an Alice band by day, or draped over a simple LBD (probably Calvin Klein) with pointed black slingbacks (probably Prada) into the night. Kate Moss, too, favored the style in her early Soho days, often opting for a cashmere camel iteration.

For fall/winter 2026, the coat shape was a key style on the runway. Jil Sander, unsurprisingly, remains something of an authority on the subject, offering a multitude of interpretations, from extra-long and oversized to collarless and polished leather styles. Elsewhere, designers have found ways to disrupt the coat’s pared-back credentials. Dries Van Noten introduced a satin finish and statement pixelated graphic, while Miu Miu did what Miu Miu does best and took the familiar shape, rendered it in crumpled leather and added a fuzzy faux-fur trim.

Unlike more statement-making outerwear that often dominates the discourse, a well-cut, single-breasted coat does a lot with very little, whether layered over tailoring for the office, worn with jeans and loafers at the weekend or thrown over eveningwear as the nights draw in.

Look for a shape that falls below the knee, a relatively clean shoulder line and enough room to accommodate a knit underneath, without swamping you when worn with bare arms. Of course, wool and cashmere styles will earn their keep on colder days, but lighter cotton versions make a useful option for milder weather and transitional dressing.

The long-line ’90s coat makes a convincing case for buying less, but buying well. Scroll on to discover our edit of the best minimalist coats to shop now.
